Estimate the value of ⟨σ​v⟩0\langle\sigma v\rangle_{0} required to the saturate the observed DM relic density. What is the predicted annihilation rate for indirect detection searches in the Milky Way, compared to ss-wave annihilation cross section above?

II.3.1  Implications for DM models

Next, let us ponder on the implications of Eq. 33 for model-building and the resulting restrictions on DM mass range. We will take as an illustrative example annihilation that occurs through an ss-channel mediator with mass mVm_{V} (remaining for the moment agnostic as to the identity of VV):

where the vector VV has coupling gχg_{\chi} with the DM and coupling gfg_{f} with the final state fermions. We will neglect the mass of the final state fermions, as before. In the non-relativistic limit, the cross section for this process is given by

σ=∫d​Ωcm​|𝐩f|16​π2​Ecm3​|𝐯1−𝐯2|​|ℳ|2=∫d​Ωcm​1|𝐯1−𝐯2|​|ℳ|232​π2​s\displaystyle\sigma=\int d\Omega_{\rm cm}\,\frac{|{\bf p}_{f}|}{16\pi^{2}E_{\rm cm}^{3}|{\bf v}_{1}-{\bf v}_{2}|}|{\cal M}|^{2}=\int d\Omega_{\rm cm}\,\frac{1}{|{\bf v}_{1}-{\bf v}_{2}|}\frac{|{\cal M}|^{2}}{32\pi^{2}s} (35)

where Ωcm\Omega_{\rm cm} are center of mass scattering angles, the center of mass energy is s=Ecm2=4​mχ2+O⁡(mχ​T)+…s=E_{\rm cm}^{2}=4m_{\chi}^{2}+O(m_{\chi}T)+..., and we used that |𝐩f|≈Ecm/2|{\bf p}_{f}|\approx E_{\rm cm}/2 in the limit of massless fermions ff. Using this result, we can approximate the thermally averaged ⟨σ​v⟩\langle\sigma v\rangle for annihilation by

⟨σ​v⟩≃|ℳ|232​π​mχ2.\displaystyle\langle\sigma v\rangle\simeq\frac{|{\cal M}|^{2}}{32\pi m_{\chi}^{2}}. (36)

Assuming Dirac fermion DM, a single flavor/color of the fermion, and a vector mediator, the spin-averaged matrix element squared of the process is given by

|ℳ|2≈gχ2​gf2​32​mχ4(s−mV2)2\displaystyle|{\cal M}|^{2}\approx g_{\chi}^{2}g_{f}^{2}\frac{32m_{\chi}^{4}}{(s-m_{V}^{2})^{2}} (37)

in the nonrelativistic limit.

  • •

    mV>mχm_{V}>m_{\chi}: In this case, the heavy VV state generates a four-fermion interaction with amplitude gχ​gf/mV2g_{\chi}g_{f}/m_{V}^{2}. The annihilation cross section can be estimated as

    ⟨σ​v⟩≃16​π​αχ​αf​mχ2mV4\displaystyle\langle\sigma v\rangle\simeq\frac{16\pi\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{f}m_{\chi}^{2}}{m_{V}^{4}} (38)

    with αχ≡gχ2/(4​π)\alpha_{\chi}\equiv g_{\chi}^{2}/(4\pi) and αf≡gf2/(4​π)\alpha_{f}\equiv g_{f}^{2}/(4\pi).

  • •

    mV<mχm_{V}<m_{\chi}: We find that the annihilation χ​χ¯→f​f¯\chi\bar{\chi}\to f\bar{f} is:

    ⟨σ​v⟩≃π​αχ​αfmχ2.\displaystyle\langle\sigma v\rangle\simeq\frac{\pi\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{f}}{m_{\chi}^{2}}. (39)

    However, a new process is then kinematically allowed, χ​χ¯→V​V\chi\bar{\chi}\to VV. If mV≪mχm_{V}\ll m_{\chi} then the only mass scale in the problem is mχm_{\chi} and we obtain:

    ⟨σ​v⟩χ​χ¯→V​V≃π​αχ2mχ2.\displaystyle\langle\sigma v\rangle_{\chi\bar{\chi}\to VV}\simeq\frac{\pi\alpha_{\chi}^{2}}{m_{\chi}^{2}}. (40)

    If αχ≫αf\alpha_{\chi}\gg\alpha_{f}, then the relic abundance may be primarily determined by this latter process. The “secluded" scenario is where αχ≫αf\alpha_{\chi}\gg\alpha_{f} and where VV is a new mediator not already present in the Standard Model [44]. Then we may regard the χ\chi and VV states as comprising a “dark sector”, and couplings to the SM thermal bath are not important for thermal freezeout.

We find, generally, that the thermally-averaged cross section is bounded from above by

⟨σ​v⟩≲π​max​(αχ​αf,αχ2)mχ2\displaystyle\langle\sigma v\rangle\lesssim\frac{\pi\ \textrm{max}(\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{f},\alpha_{\chi}^{2})}{m_{\chi}^{2}} (41)

since for the case mV>mχm_{V}>m_{\chi} there is an additional suppression in the cross section by (mχ/mV)4(m_{\chi}/m_{V})^{4}. (An exception is if there is a resonance in the ss-channel, mV≈2​mχm_{V}\approx 2m_{\chi}.)

If the desired cross section is that of Eq. 33, then there are a few important lessons to draw from this. First, one can set an upper bound on the DM mass, if we assume perturbative couplings – this is also known as a perturbative unitarity bound [34]. Taking αχ,f→1\alpha_{\chi,f}\to 1 in Eq. 41 then gives

mχ≲50−100​TeV.\displaystyle m_{\chi}\lesssim 50-100\ \textrm{TeV}. (42)

More specific bounds can be obtained in particular models [45]. The basic idea is that a heavier DM candidate that was in thermal equilibrium could not annihilate away sufficiently, resulting in an overabundance of DM. We already alluded to the fact that there are possible exceptions to this analysis, and we will return to this in Sec. II.4.

The second lesson is that a TeV-scale DM candidate is a viable possibility, where αχ,f\alpha_{\chi,f} can be on the order 10−2−10−110^{-2}-10^{-1}. Indeed, the WIMP miracle is the observation that ⟨σ​v⟩\langle\sigma v\rangle above can be rewritten in the form:

⟨σ​v⟩≈αw21​TeV2\displaystyle\langle\sigma v\rangle\approx\frac{\alpha_{w}^{2}}{1\,{\rm TeV}^{2}} (43)

with αw≈0.03\alpha_{w}\approx 0.03 for S​U​(2)LSU(2)_{L} weak interactions. This is an inviting cross section for particle theorists accustomed to the sizes of the SM gauge couplings and to thinking about extensions of the SM at the TeV scale. Indeed, thermal candidates that are electroweak multiplets (such as a pure Higgsino in supersymmetric extensions of the SM) remain compelling DM candidates [46, 47, 48, 49, 50]. In the most minimal scenario, no other new particles or gauge interactions are required for TeV thermal relics.

II.3.2  Mediators for light DM

In turning to lighter DM below the weak scale, the minimalist approach becomes insufficient at a certain point. Let us take VV to be a weak scale mediator, which could be the Higgs or an EW gauge boson. We have a cross section given by Eq. 38, which can be rewritten as

⟨σ​v⟩≈mχ2GeV2​αχ​αfαw2​1109​GeV2\displaystyle\langle\sigma v\rangle\approx\frac{m_{\chi}^{2}}{\textrm{GeV}^{2}}\frac{\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{f}}{\alpha_{w}^{2}}\frac{1}{10^{9}\,\textrm{GeV}^{2}} (44)

where we have taken mV≈100​GeVm_{V}\approx 100\ \textrm{GeV}. If the couplings are the weak gauge couplings, αχ​αf=αw2\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{f}=\alpha_{w}^{2}, then the cross section drops below the desired thermal relic cross section when mχ<GeVm_{\chi}<\textrm{GeV}. Weak interactions would thus lead to an overabundance of sub-GeV DM, a conclusion commonly known as the Lee-Weinberg bound [51].

The implication is that for sub-GeV DM, new mediators below the weak scale are required. But wait – there is one more candidate for VV in the Standard Model, the photon. Since mV≪mχm_{V}\ll m_{\chi}, the Lee-Weinberg bound does not apply. Although this would appear to go against the notion of dark matter as “dark”, we must work through this possibility in a more quantitative way.

Consider a DM candidate which has a small, fractional electric charge Q≪1Q\ll 1, otherwise known as a millicharged or minicharged DM candidate.66 6 For a discussion of specific models realizing this, see for example Refs. [52, 53, 54]. The annihilation cross section χ¯​χ→f​f¯\bar{\chi}\chi\to f\bar{f} for a single charged species ff is given by ⟨σ​v⟩≈π​αem2​Q2/mχ2\langle\sigma v\rangle\approx\pi\alpha_{\rm em}^{2}Q^{2}/m_{\chi}^{2}; this should be summed over all final states with appropriate final state charges and color factors. Neglecting such factors for the purpose of estimation, one finds that

Q≃10−3​(mχGeV)\displaystyle Q\simeq 10^{-3}\left(\frac{m_{\chi}}{\textrm{GeV}}\right) (45)

in order to obtain the desired thermal relic cross section. This time χ¯​χ→γ​γ\bar{\chi}\chi\to\gamma\gamma can be neglected since the cross section has an additional Q2Q^{2} suppression. Furthermore, we ought to require mχ>mem_{\chi}>m_{e} for there to be a final state to annihilate into.

Such charges can potentially be constrained in accelerator experiments. However, the strongest test of charged DM arises from its behavior in the early universe. At redshifts z≳1000z\gtrsim 1000, the universe was mostly ionized in the form of free protons and electrons. A millicharged DM candidate can scatter off the protons and electrons with a Rutherford-type cross section, leading to both a suppression of the growth of DM structure [55] as well as a DM-baryon drag force which leaves an imprint on the CMB anisotropies [56, 57, 58, 59]. We can obtain an estimate of the bound arising from the first effect, although the second effect leads to an even stronger constraint over the entire mass range [57].

DM-baryon scattering has a Rutherford-type cross section given by d​σ/d​Ω=Q2​αem2/(4​μχ​f​v2​sin2⁡(θ/2))2d\sigma/d\Omega=Q^{2}\alpha_{\rm em}^{2}/\left(4\mu_{\chi f}v^{2}\sin^{2}(\theta/2)\right)^{2}, where μχ​f\mu_{\chi f} is the DM-baryon reduced mass and vv is the relative velocity. This scattering rate diverges in the θ→0\theta\to 0 limit and is regulated by a Debye screening angle θD≡mD/(μχ​f​v)\theta_{D}\equiv m_{D}/(\mu_{\chi f}v), with the Debye mass given by mD=4​π​α​ne/Tγ≈4×10−6​Tγm_{D}=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha n_{e}/T_{\gamma}}\approx 4\times 10^{-6}\,T_{\gamma}. Furthermore, in the limit of forward scattering the momentum transfer between the DM and baryon goes to zero. As a result, the physically relevant quantity is the transfer cross section σT\sigma_{T}, defined as:

σT≡∫d​Ω​d​σd​Ω​(1−cos⁡θ)=4​π​Q2​αem2μχ​f2​v4​log⁡(2θD).\displaystyle\sigma_{T}\equiv\int d\Omega\,\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(1-\cos\theta)=\frac{4\pi Q^{2}\alpha^{2}_{\rm em}}{\mu_{\chi f}^{2}v^{4}}\log\left(\frac{2}{\theta_{D}}\right)\,. (46)
  • ⋆\star

    Exercise: Consider a gas of DM particles (with temperature TT) incident with average velocity 𝐕{\bf V} on a gas of protons with the same temperature. Assuming nonrelativistic particles, what is the momentum transfer in a single collision? Average over the DM and proton velocity distributions to obtain the force mχ​d​𝐕/d​tm_{\chi}d{\bf V}/dt experienced by the DM gas, and show that it is proportional to the transfer cross section.

We now make a number of approximations in order to obtain a quick estimate. Let us focus on DM-proton scattering, since the transfer cross section scales as 1/v41/v^{4} and the protons are much slower moving than the electrons. Next, for sub-GeV DM we can take μχ​p≈mχ\mu_{\chi p}\approx m_{\chi}. For the velocities we can make a few choices: we can assume that the relative velocities vv are dominated by the baryon thermal velocities, v∼Tγ/mpv\sim\sqrt{T_{\gamma}/m_{p}}, while the DM is much colder. Alternatively, we can assume that the DM is at a similar temperature, in which case v∼Tγ/mχv\sim\sqrt{T_{\gamma}/m_{\chi}} since the DM is much lighter. Since the cross section is inversely proportional to v4v^{4}, we will make the conservative assumption that v∼Tγ/mχv\sim\sqrt{T_{\gamma}/m_{\chi}} because this suppresses the scattering rate and will give the weakest constraint (this was the case considered in Ref. [55]). Finally, because the Debye angle θD\theta_{D} is usually tiny, we approximate the forward scattering log as log⁡2θD∼O⁡(10)\log\tfrac{2}{\theta_{D}}\sim O(10). Then the rate per DM particle is

Γ=np​⟨σ​v⟩≈6×10−10​nγ​40​π​Q2​αem2mχ​Tγ3≈10−8​Q2​αem2​Tγ3mχ\displaystyle\Gamma=n_{p}\langle\sigma v\rangle\approx 6\times 10^{-10}\,n_{\gamma}\frac{40\pi Q^{2}\alpha^{2}_{\rm em}}{\sqrt{m_{\chi}T_{\gamma}^{3}}}\approx 10^{-8}\,Q^{2}\alpha^{2}_{\rm em}\sqrt{\frac{T_{\gamma}^{3}}{m_{\chi}}} (47)

Here we used that the baryon-to-photon asymmetry is η≈6×10−10\eta\approx 6\times 10^{-10} and nγ≈Tγ3/4n_{\gamma}\approx T_{\gamma}^{3}/4.

We will compare the rate against the Hubble expansion at Tγ≈T_{\gamma}\approx eV: at these temperatures, we are well within the epoch where we require DM structure formation to proceed according to Λ\LambdaCDM. At this time, the universe is just barely still radiation dominated and using H≈Tγ2/MplH\approx T_{\gamma}^{2}/M_{\rm pl}, we find that Γ/H≪1\Gamma/H\ll 1 implies

Q≪2×10−6​(mχGeV)1/4\displaystyle Q\ll 2\times 10^{-6}\left(\frac{m_{\chi}}{\textrm{GeV}}\right)^{1/4} (48)

This bound excludes the charges needed for a thermal relic, given in Eq. 45 for mχ>mem_{\chi}>m_{e}.

Concluding our survey of millicharged DM, we return to the main point: a model for sub-GeV DM which obtains its relic abundance by thermal freezeout generically requires additional new sub-GeV states for sufficient DM annihilation. We have shown that the SM electroweak gauge bosons and photon are not viable possibilities. (We have not discussed the strong force, as there are even more experimental constraints!) This will motivate the study of dark sectors for sub-GeV DM, that contain both the DM and other light states. The excess of energy and entropy density in a dark sector may be excluded by other cosmological considerations, requiring that the excess be deposited back into the SM thermal bath. As a result, we will often consider new light mediators to the SM. We will explore these arguments in more detail in Lecture 3.

II.4  Many miracles

The discussion up to this point has motivated thermal DM with relic abundance set by annihilations, viable in the mass range of keV up to 100 TeV. Within this mass range, the “magic number” of Eq. 33 and the WIMP miracle seems like a wonderful coincidence in scales, and suggestive of a physics connection. But it is a coincidence between two model paradigms, not two demonstrated phenomena. Let’s see what happens when we examine more closely some of the assumptions leading to Eq. 33:

  • •

    No chemical potential. It was assumed that the annihilation rate is proportional to the equilibrium number density of χ\chi particles, but there could be an asymmetry in the number density of χ\chi and χ¯\bar{\chi}, similar to the baryons. The relic density then depends on both the annihilation rate and the asymmetry [60, 61]. An additional appeal of asymmetric DM models [62] that they can explain why Ωc\Omega_{c} is of the same order as the baryon density Ωb\Omega_{b}.

  • •

    No resonances or threshold behavior. It is assumed that the cross section is approximately constant throughout freezeout. The presence of threshold behavior or resonances leads to a strong TT-dependence in the cross section, affecting the desired couplings (see for example Ref. [63] on “three exceptions” to the standard freezeout story).

  • •

    Annihilations of DM DM →\to SM SM interactions dominate. The annihilation rate is proportional to one power of the DM density with this assumption. Exceptions include co-annihilation, where DM annihilates against another (heavier) state [63]; co-scattering [64], where inelastic DM scattering processes determine the relic abundance; and SIMP [65] models where 3→23\to 2 annihilations are most important in setting the relic density. If the annihilation is DM DM DM →\to DM DM, this can be considered an example cannibal DM [66, 67], where the dark sector consumes itself to stay warm.

  • •

    Annihilation during the radiation-dominated era in the standard cosmology. A long-lived massive particle present in the early universe could result in a matter dominated era. If freezeout occurs during this era, then the annihilation cross section could in principle be much smaller, since the DM density is diluted after the decay of the massive particle. Examples include Refs. [68, 69]. Note that this could also be applied to get around the need for new light mediators for sub-GeV thermal candidates.

The list goes on. All of these have been applied in dark sector models, showing the great breadth of freezeout phenomenology.

So far we have outlined ways to decrease YfoY_{\rm fo}, motivated by the overabundance of any massive particle that was relativistic as freezeout. Of course, another way to suppress YfoY_{\rm fo} is if the DM had never been in equilibrium in the early universe. The difficulty with this scenario is that the relic abundance can be quite sensitive to initial conditions (UV-dominated) and other assumptions at early times. However, it is possible to have a non-thermal DM candidate that is not UV-dominated, and potentially observable direct detection experiment. In the remainder of this section, we describe this candidate.

II.4.1  Freeze-in

There is one more scenario, which strictly speaking is not a thermal candidate. Freeze-in [70] is a mechanism whereby rare interactions within the SM thermal bath slowly build up an abundance of DM. (In the usual freeze-in story, it is thus assumed that dark sector particles are not produced at an appreciable level through decay of the inflaton during reheating.) As a specific example, let’s look at freeze-in by ss-channel annihilation of SM particles, such as e+​e−e^{+}e^{-}, into DM particles. The coupling of the DM particles is assumed to be sufficiently feeble, that the reaction is never in equilibrium.

In the “UV-dominated” scenario, the production cross section depends on a high scale Λ\Lambda; for example, for scalar DM the interaction is a dimension-5 operator which we can parameterize as gχ​ge​vHΛ2​χ2​e¯​e\tfrac{g_{\chi}g_{e}v_{H}}{\Lambda^{2}}\chi^{2}\bar{e}e. We have included the factor of the Higgs vacuum expectation value, vH=246v_{H}=246 GeV, to account for the fact that the operator is not S​U​(2)LSU(2)_{L} invariant. Then the cross section goes as

⟨σ​v⟩≃αχ​αe​vH2Λ4.\displaystyle\langle\sigma v\rangle\simeq\frac{\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{e}v_{H}^{2}}{\Lambda^{4}}. (49)

The rate of producing a DM particle per electron is Γe+​e−→χ​χ=ne​⟨σ​v⟩∼αχ​αe​T3​vH2/Λ4\Gamma_{e^{+}e^{-}\to\chi\chi}=n_{e}\langle\sigma v\rangle\sim\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{e}T^{3}v_{H}^{2}/\Lambda^{4}\, for T≫me,mχT\gg m_{e},m_{\chi}. Thus, the number of DM particles created per electron in a Hubble time is Γ​H−1\Gamma H^{-1}. The abundance of total newly-created DM at any given time is

Yχ=nχs≃ne​Γ​H−1s≃Γg∗,S​H≃αχ​αe​vH2​Mpl​Tg∗​g∗,S​Λ4,\displaystyle Y_{\chi}=\frac{n_{\chi}}{s}\simeq\frac{n_{e}\Gamma H^{-1}}{s}\simeq\frac{\Gamma}{g_{*,S}\,H}\simeq\frac{\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{e}\,v_{H}^{2}\,M_{\rm pl}T}{\sqrt{g_{*}}g_{*,S}\,\Lambda^{4}}, (50)

with the greatest abundance produced at the highest TT (as long as T<ΛT<\Lambda). The relic density is sensitive to the reheating of the universe and the maximum available temperatures. Assuming that this process gives all of the dark matter and requiring that the highest T>MeVT>\textrm{MeV} and mχ>keVm_{\chi}>\textrm{keV} gives a lower bound on Λ/(αχ​αe)1/4≳106​GeV\Lambda/(\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{e})^{1/4}\gtrsim 10^{6}\,\textrm{GeV}. With such high scales or small couplings, the prospects for laboratory detection in the near future are quite limited.

  • ⋆\star

    Exercise: What is the maximum DM-electron scattering cross section for this case? In order to obtain an estimate, assume an incident DM with velocity v∼10−3v\sim 10^{-3} and take the electron to be at rest. Then the electron scattering cross section is roughly σe∼μχ​e2​αχ​αe​vH2/(mχ2​Λ4)\sigma_{e}\sim\mu_{\chi e}^{2}\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{e}v_{H}^{2}/(m_{\chi}^{2}\Lambda^{4}), where μχ​e\mu_{\chi e} is the DM-electron reduced mass. What if we instead consider a dimension-6 operator (the heavy VV limit of the vector interaction considered earlier) for freeze-in?

On the other hand, if the mediator is lighter than the DM, then we can have “IR-dominated” freeze-in. Going back to the example introduced above Eq. 35 where DM is coupled to a light vector mediator, the production cross section for e+​e−→χ​χ¯e^{+}e^{-}\to\chi\bar{\chi} has the form

⟨σ​v⟩≃αχ​αeT2\displaystyle\langle\sigma v\rangle\simeq\frac{\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{e}}{T^{2}} (51)

in the limit of mV≪mχm_{V}\ll m_{\chi}. Similar to above, the comoving abundance of total newly-created DM is given by

Yχ=nχs≈Γg∗,S​H≃αχ​αe​Mplg∗​g∗,S​T\displaystyle Y_{\chi}=\frac{n_{\chi}}{s}\approx\frac{\Gamma}{g_{*,S}\,H}\simeq\frac{\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{e}\,M_{\rm pl}}{\sqrt{g_{*}}g_{*,S}\,T} (52)

so that most of the DM is produced at around the lowest TT where the process is kinematically accessible. Either the DM becomes too heavy (T<mχT<m_{\chi}) which suppresses the production rate, or the electrons become too dilute (T<meT<m_{e}). While the total abundance should be obtained by integrating the production at all times, we can estimate the relic abudance by taking Yfo=Y⁡(T)Y_{\rm fo}=Y(T) at the lowest TT. There are two possibilities depending on the DM mass, which results in the following condition on the couplings

αχ​αe≃{g∗​g∗,S|T=mχ×eVMpl≈3×10−27−10−26,mχ>meg∗​g∗,S|T=me×eVMpl​memχ≈3×10−27×memχ,mχ<me.\displaystyle\alpha_{\chi}\alpha_{e}\simeq\begin{cases}\sqrt{g_{*}}g_{*,S}|_{T=m_{\chi}}\times\frac{\textrm{eV}}{M_{\rm pl}}\approx 3\times 10^{-27}-10^{-26},&m_{\chi}>m_{e}\\ \sqrt{g_{*}}g_{*,S}|_{T=m_{e}}\times\frac{\textrm{eV}}{M_{\rm pl}}\frac{m_{e}}{m_{\chi}}\approx 3\times 10^{-27}\times\frac{m_{e}}{m_{\chi}},&m_{\chi}<m_{e}\end{cases}. (53)

If we take the mediator to be the SM photon, this is then an example of a sub-GeV DM candidate that does not require any new mediators beyond the SM! In particular, the couplings required satisfy the bound given in Eq. 48. (Note that for mχ<mem_{\chi}<m_{e} and the SM photon as the mediator, there is an additional large production mechanism whereby the in-medium plasma oscillations can decay to χ​χ¯\chi\bar{\chi}; this modifies the coupling constants above by about an order of magnitude, depending on the mass [54].) Despite the tiny couplings, this scenario is potentially detectable with direct detection or indirect searches when the mediator mass is much smaller than the DM mass. We will explore this further in the following lectures.

In addition to freeze-in via annihilation-type processes, another possibility is freeze-in of DM through the decay of heavy particles. Since the heavy particle can have relatively larger coupling with the SM, they could be produced in colliders and decay with a long lifetime, giving an interesting observational handle of these types of freeze-in models. For studies of the long-lived particle collider signatures from freeze-in, see for example Refs. [71, 72, 73]. A recent review of freeze-in models and their associated signatures can be found in Ref. [74].

III  Dark sectors and light mediators

What we have learned from the previous lecture is that models of sub-GeV thermal relic DM generically require some new mediator states below the weak scale. This is so that there is a sufficiently large annihilation cross section, and the DM is not too abundant. The new state (and the DM itself, of course) must have a sufficiently small coupling to SM particles, otherwise we could have seen it in numerous laboratory experiments. For instance, the new state could mediate SM-SM interactions as well, and at a minimum the effects should be smaller than weak interactions. This motivates the dark sector, or hidden sector framework, where we view the DM and mediator as part of a separate “Dark Standard Model”, and where there is a portal link to the SM. If the dark sector is thermally populated during the early universe, the portal link also allows for any excess energy/entropy to be deposited back to the SM thermal bath. The ingredients of the dark sector can be fairly minimal, consisting of a feebly coupled dark force and a dark fermion charged under that force. At the other end of the spectrum of possibilities, there are composite dark sectors or a multitude of new states (such as a large number of copies of the SM).

The reasons for studying dark sectors are the following:

  • •

    They represent a theoretical generalization of thermal DM candidates beyond WIMPs or supersymmetric DM

  • •

    They provide a collection of benchmarks and useful targets for experimental tests of the thermal relic scenario

  • •

    They represent new directions in the signatures and phenomenology of DM that is driven more by the desire to expand experimental searches and data, rather than by top-down considerations such as naturalness, the strong CP problem, etc.

While we do not aim to provide a complete review of the literature, we refer the reader to the some of the well-known early works proposing dark sectors [75, 44, 76, 77] and to some recent white papers [78, 79].

Here we explore realizations of dark sectors, the implications for cosmology, and the myriad ways to search for the portal link. We begin by asking the question – is any (detectable) link to the SM required?

III.1  Cosmology of secluded sectors

In the case of a secluded sector (see Eq. 40 and below), the DM candidate χ\chi annihilates to a mediator state VV with mχ>mVm_{\chi}>m_{V}. Ostensibly, interactions with the SM are not required for thermal freezeout. However, there are interesting and strong constraints even in this scenario.

As a starting point, suppose the dark sector was populated during reheating, leaving behind a separate thermal plasma of secluded sector states that don’t interact with the SM thermal bath during freezeout. Let us call the temperature ratio between the two sectors ξ\xi:

ξ≡TdTγ,\displaystyle\xi\equiv\frac{T_{d}}{T_{\gamma}}, (54)

where this quantity is time-dependent. In order for the freezeout story to be more or less unmodified, the DM must interact with a relativistic thermal bath. If mV≪mχm_{V}\ll m_{\chi}, then the thermal population of VV itself could play this role. An alternative simple extension is to introduce an additional light species νD\nu_{D} in the dark sector, where mχ>mV≫mνDm_{\chi}>m_{V}\gg m_{\nu_{D}}. The annihilation processes for these two possibilities is shown in Fig. 7.

  • ⋆\star

    Exercise: How are the estimates of relic abundance modified for this secluded sector? As part of this exercise, determine how the relic abundance calculation changes when ξ≠1\xi\neq 1.

The excess entropy and energy density in the dark sector must go somewhere, however. Suppose VV is stable, as in the first scenario in Fig. 7. Then VV is a component of the total dark matter relic density, with a number density proportional to ξ3​T3\xi^{3}T^{3}. Assuming that ξ∼O⁡(1)\xi\sim O(1), we can use Using Eq. 26 as a guide for the relic abundance in VV. Then if mV≫m_{V}\gg eV, there would be an overabundance of DM, but for mVm_{V} on the order of eV there would be a non-negligible quantity of hot DM. As a result, it must be that mV≪m_{V}\ll eV. (For more quantitative bounds on specific hot DM scenarios, see for example Ref. [80].) It is then the case that VV behaves as an additional component of radiation during the early universe.

The presence of additional radiation during BBN or recombination leaves an imprint on the light element abundances and the CMB power spectrum. Any free-streaming radiation not contained in the photon bath is usually encapsulated in the quantity NeffN_{\textrm{eff}}, the effective number of relativistic degrees of freedom. At leading order, the relevant quantity is the energy density in this relativistic species, so let us write down the total energy density in radiation, including neutrinos while they are still relativistic:

ρtot\displaystyle\rho_{\rm tot} =2​π230​Tγ4+7​NeffSM4​π230​Tν4+ρd\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi^{2}}{30}\,T_{\gamma}^{4}+\frac{7N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm SM}}{4}\frac{\pi^{2}}{30}\,T_{\nu}^{4}+\rho_{d} (55)

where ρd\rho_{d} is the dark sector contribution. The second term is from neutrinos, using Eq. 17 with g=2g=2. Recall that in the instantaneous decoupling approximation that Tν=(4/11)1/3​TγT_{\nu}=(4/11)^{1/3}T_{\gamma} is the neutrino temperature after electron decoupling in the standard cosmology. In the standard model, NeffSM≈3.046N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm SM}\approx 3.046, accounting for deviations from instantaneous decoupling.

Additional sources of radiation are parametrized by Δ​Neff\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}, the deviation in NeffN_{\textrm{eff}} from the standard model value. Assuming that the neutrino temperature is the same as in the SM, then

ρtot≡ργ+(NeffSM+Δ​Neff)​74​π230​Tν4.\displaystyle\rho_{\rm tot}\equiv\rho_{\gamma}+\left(N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm SM}+\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}\right)\frac{7}{4}\frac{\pi^{2}}{30}\,T_{\nu}^{4}\ . (56)

For the dark sector, this implies

ρd=∑igi​π230​Ti4→Δ​Neff=47​∑igi​(TiTν)4,\rho_{d}=\sum_{i}g_{i}\frac{\pi^{2}}{30}T_{i}^{4}\quad\rightarrow\quad\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}=\frac{4}{7}\sum_{i}g_{i}\left(\frac{T_{i}}{T_{\nu}}\right)^{4}, (57)

where gig_{i} and TiT_{i} are the effective degrees of freedom and the temperature of the various relativistic species in the dark sector.

Clearly, Δ​Neff\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}} is a time-dependent quantity, while the constraints are at specific epochs: Δ​NeffBBN\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm BBN} is the energy density in radiation for T∼10​keV−1​MeVT\sim 10\,\textrm{keV}-1\,\textrm{MeV} and Δ​NeffCMB\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm CMB} is the energy density T<eVT<\,\textrm{eV} for Δ​NeffCMB\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm CMB}. At the time of writing, BBN abundance measurements [81] and Planck observations of the CMB (combined with baryon acoustic oscillations) indicate [38], respectively,

NeffBBN\displaystyle N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm BBN} =2.89±0.28\displaystyle=2.89\pm 0.28 (58)
NeffCMB\displaystyle N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm CMB} =2.99±0.17\displaystyle=2.99\pm 0.17 (59)

It is important to note that the central values depend on the particular dataset and assumed parameters, while the error bars are also quite model-dependent. For instance, accounting for a possible mass scale in the neutrino/dark sector, or strong self-interactions can lead to error bars larger by an O⁡(1)O(1) factor. Accounting for possible model independence, this roughly indicates that currently |Δ​NeffBBN,CMB|≲0.5−0.7|\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm BBN,CMB}|\lesssim 0.5-0.7 at the 2σ\sigma level.

It is exciting to note that measurements of NeffN_{\textrm{eff}} will improve significantly with future CMB observations. The target CMB-S4 sensitivity is σ⁡(Δ​Neff)≈0.03\sigma(\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}})\approx 0.03 [82]. This is remarkable because it is a probe of any relativistic degree of freedom that was in equilibrium with the SM thermal bath, up to the QCD phase transition (or even up to the EW phase transition, for fermions or vectors).

What does this mean specifically for dark sector models? Let us take as an example a fairly minimal secluded scenario, where all the degrees of freedom are scalars (to have the smallest gg). Suppose equilibrium was established at some early time by some higher dimension operator, but the two thermal baths later decoupled at a temperature Td​e​cT_{dec}. We assume that the decoupling is well before BBN, and occurs when the DM is still relativistic. The minimum energy density in the dark sector at this time was

ρdm​i​n​(Td​e​c)=2​π230​Td​e​c4\displaystyle\rho_{d}^{min}(T_{dec})=\frac{2\pi^{2}}{30}T_{dec}^{4} (60)

where we have taken 2 as the minimum number of degrees of freedom, for one scalar DM and one scalar mediator state. At decoupling, we may assume T=Tγ=TνT=T_{\gamma}=T_{\nu} but afterward the two thermal baths evolve separately.

For the sake of being concrete, suppose that the mass of both the DM and mediator are below the MeV scale, so that we may assume they are relativistic at T=MeVT=\textrm{MeV}. As the universe cools, massive particles are annihilating away in the SM thermal bath, so that there is a relative increase in the photon+neutrino temperature by [g∗SM​(Td​e​c)/g∗SM​(MeV)]1/3\left[g_{*}^{\rm SM}(T_{dec})/g_{*}^{\rm SM}(\textrm{MeV})\right]^{1/3} from Td​e​cT_{dec} until neutrino decoupling. Here g∗SM​(T)g_{*}^{\rm SM}(T) refers to the effective number of relativistic SM degrees of freedom, shown in Fig. 5. To find Δ​Neff\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}, we track the dark sector temperature relative to the neutrino temperature:

ρdm​i​n​(MeV)=2​π230​Tν4​[g∗SM​(MeV)g∗SM​(Td​e​c)]4/3.\displaystyle\rho_{d}^{min}(\textrm{MeV})=\frac{2\pi^{2}}{30}T_{\nu}^{4}\left[\frac{g_{*}^{\rm SM}(\textrm{MeV})}{g_{*}^{\rm SM}(T_{dec})}\right]^{4/3}. (61)

Comparing with Eq. 56, we obtain a value of Δ​NeffBBN=0.053\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm BBN}=0.053 if Td​e​c>200T_{dec}>200 GeV. This is a minimum value of Δ​NeffBBN\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm BBN}, assuming there are no other degrees of freedom that are in equilibrium with the SM. Fig. 8 shows Δ​NeffBBN\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm BBN} as a function of Td​e​cT_{dec}.

Below T∼MeVT\sim\textrm{MeV}, the neutrino temperature redshifts in the standard cosmology. However, life still goes on in the dark sector. At some point, the DM freezes out by annihilation to the mediator states, with the number of degrees of freedom changing from 2 to 1. Entropy is conserved in this process, leading to a relative increase in the dark sector temperature by 21/32^{1/3}. Therefore the energy density at the time of recombination is

ρdm​i​n​(Trec)=π230​Tν4​24/3​[g∗SM​(MeV)g∗SM​(Td​e​c)]4/3\displaystyle\rho_{d}^{min}(T_{\rm rec})=\frac{\pi^{2}}{30}T_{\nu}^{4}2^{4/3}\left[\frac{g_{*}^{\rm SM}(\textrm{MeV})}{g_{*}^{\rm SM}(T_{dec})}\right]^{4/3} (62)

giving Δ​NeffCMB=0.067\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm CMB}=0.067 if Td​e​c>200T_{dec}>200 GeV! Again, this Fig. 8 shows Δ​Neff\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}} as a function of Td​e​cT_{dec}, comparing the values at CMB and BBN. Even this minimal scenario could lead to an observable Δ​NeffCMB\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm CMB} with CMB-S4!

The lesson to be drawn from this is that future cosmological datasets will provide a strong test of the secluded dark sector through gravitational effects. However, this is no guarantee: a null result could be consistent with a high Td​e​cT_{dec}, the presence of additional degrees of freedom in equilibrium with the SM thermal bath (e.g. in a supersymmetric model), or a modified cosmology. For example, Ref. [83] explores the limitations on reheating scenarios that can populate a secluded sector consistent with bounds on NeffN_{\textrm{eff}}. A positive detection of Δ​Neff\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}, conversely, is not necessarily a signature of DM. But it would be strongly suggestive of a light relic that decoupled from the SM thermal bath before BBN, thus giving a probe into a new regime of the early universe.

We leave it as an exercise to determine Δ​NeffCMB\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm CMB} for a secluded sector consisting of Dirac fermion DM and vector mediator. Additional dark sector scenarios for Δ​Neff\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}} can be found Refs. [84, 85, 86, 87, 88, 89]. There are also phenomenological possibilities beyond just Δ​NeffCMB\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm CMB} and Δ​NeffBBN\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}}^{\rm BBN}. For a study of how time-dependent Δ​Neff\Delta N_{\textrm{eff}} during BBN affects light element abundances, see Ref. [90]. In addition, an interacting relativistic dark sector has a different imprint on the CMB compared to free-streaming dark sector radiation [91].

III.1.1  DM self-interactions

Interactions within the dark sector can also be imprinted in the clustering of DM. Self-scattering of DM, shown in Fig. 9a, can lead to thermalization of DM in halos, suppression of small scale structure, and a reduction of central densities within galaxies and galaxy clusters. Indeed, self-interacting DM (SIDM) was originally proposed [92] in order to explain the “cusp vs. core” problem, where the central profiles of dwarf galaxies were observed to be much shallower than predicted in DM-only simulations, and the “missing satellites” problem, where the observed number of satellites of the Milky Way appeared to be far too low. Recent work has also pointed out the related “too big to fail” [93] and “diversity of rotation curves” [94, 95] problems. Improvements in simulations that include baryons suggest that baryonic physics may be sufficient to explain the halo profiles of dwarfs, and more satellites are now being discovered. Still, DM self-interactions remain an intriguing way to explain other properties of galaxies, and the predictions for SIDM in the presence of baryons are still being understood; for a recent review, see Ref. [96].

A figure of merit for when self-interactions are important is when the transfer cross section σ\sigma (cross section weighted by momentum transfer, see definition in Eq. 46) over DM mass has a typical value of

σ/mχ∼1​cm2g=2×10−24​cm2​(GeVmχ).\displaystyle\sigma/m_{\chi}\sim 1\frac{{\rm cm}^{2}}{\rm g}=2\times 10^{-24}{\rm cm}^{2}\,\left(\frac{\rm GeV}{m_{\chi}}\right)\,. (63)

Assuming a typical DM density ρDM≈\rho_{\rm DM}\approx GeV/cm3 and DM velocity v∼10−3v\sim 10^{-3}, this gives a scattering rate per DM particle

Γ≈ρDMmχ​σ​v≈1109​year.\displaystyle\Gamma\approx\frac{\rho_{\rm DM}}{m_{\chi}}\sigma v\approx\frac{1}{10^{9}\,{\rm year}}. (64)

The dynamical time scale for a typical MW-like galaxy or its massive subhalos is around 108−10910^{8}-10^{9} years, so this is around the cross section needed to affect the halo dynamics. In the inner regions of halos, the interaction rate can be significantly higher.

DM scattering via light mediators can easily give rise to such large cross sections. As a result, self-interactions are an important constraint on low mass dark sectors and especially the secluded scenario where, by definition, the mediator is lighter than the DM, mV<mχm_{V}<m_{\chi}. Specifically, consider the secluded scenario with an ultralight mediator with mass mV≪eVm_{V}\ll\textrm{eV}, shown in the left panel of Fig. 7. In this limit, self-interactions are especially restrictive. Since mV≪mχ​vm_{V}\ll m_{\chi}v for mχ≳keVm_{\chi}\gtrsim\textrm{keV}, there is a forward scattering enhancement and the Born limit for the transfer cross section is given by

σ≈8​π​αχ2mχ2​v4​ln⁡(mχ​v)2mV2.\displaystyle\sigma\approx\frac{8\pi\alpha_{\chi}^{2}}{m_{\chi}^{2}v^{4}}\ln\frac{(m_{\chi}v)^{2}}{m_{V}^{2}}. (65)

αχ=gχ2/(4​π)\alpha_{\chi}=g_{\chi}^{2}/(4\pi) is the coupling of the DM with the mediator and the specific numerical prefactor depends on the spin of the DM and mediator. Taking σ<1​cm2/g\sigma<1{\rm cm}^{2}/{\rm g}, this translates to an SIDM bound of

αχ≲few×10−10​(v10−3)2​(mχMeV)3/2​(10ln⁡(mχ2​v2/mV2))1/2.\displaystyle\alpha_{\chi}\lesssim{\rm few}\times 10^{-10}\left(\frac{v}{10^{-3}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{m_{\chi}}{\textrm{MeV}}\right)^{3/2}\left(\frac{10}{\ln(m_{\chi}^{2}v^{2}/m_{V}^{2})}\right)^{1/2}. (66)

Now, if we compare with the couplings needed to set the relic abundance, the SIDM constraint excludes thermal freezeout if mχm_{\chi} is below the GeV scale.

  • ⋆\star

    Exercise: Using the annihilation cross section given in Eq. 40, verify the above statement that thermal freezeout via annihilation into an ultralight mediator (left panel of Fig. 7) is strongly constrained by self-interactions in galaxies.

Of course, there are ways around these conclusions. If there is a large splitting for the Dirac fermion, then self-interactions are kinematically suppressed. For a discussion of self-scattering for inelastic DM, see for example Refs. [97, 98, 99]. Alternatively, additional hidden sector states could be introduced for thermal freeze-out of sub-GeV secluded sectors, for example with processes such as that shown in the right panel of Fig. 7. Then it is not necessary to take the ultralight mV≪eVm_{V}\ll\textrm{eV} limit. If the mediator mass mV≫mχ​vm_{V}\gg m_{\chi}v, then the self-interaction cross section can be estimated as σ≈π​αχ2​mχ2/mV4\sigma\approx\pi\alpha_{\chi}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}/m_{V}^{4}. Then SIDM bounds are still an important consideration for dark sector models, but much less restrictive. in particular, it does not exclude the possibility of thermal freezeout.

In the above discussion, we have considered the scattering cross section only in a few limits where the Born approximation is valid. In the general parameter space of αχ,mV,\alpha_{\chi},m_{V},and mχm_{\chi}, there are additional resonant enhancement effects and one must solve the general quantum mechanical scattering problem. A number of works have considered the parameter space of αχ,mV,mχ\alpha_{\chi},m_{V},m_{\chi}, subject to the requirement of explaining the DM relic density [101, 102]. Interestingly, a combined fit to the halo properties across a range of velocity dispersions (from dwarf galaxies to galaxy clusters) has found preferred parameters of DM with mass ∼10\sim 10 GeV and scattering through mediator with mass ∼10\sim 10 MeV [100]. This is shown in Fig. 10. (See Ref. [103] for the best fits in the asymmetric DM case.) The results were obtained in analytic models of SIDM halos, and there is much to be done in interpreting observations of galaxies. At the order of magnitude level, Fig. 10 also gives a useful summary of the typical cross sections allowed in various astrophysical systems, since we expect the cross section cannot be significantly larger than their best fit.

Finally, let us briefly discuss DM sector interactions in the early universe. If there are dark sector states that were relativistic during the early universe, then DM scattering can lead to dark acoustic oscillations. An example is shown in Fig. 9b, where the νD\nu_{D} is a sub-eV relativistic particle. The presence of sizeable self-interactions may then be tied to CMB or large scale structure signatures. For example, Ref. [103] has explored the predictions for dark acoustic oscillations within the SIDM parameter space, focusing on a minimal secluded dark sector with dark radiation. Another example is atomic dark matter [104], where the dark sector consists of a dark proton, a dark electron, and a dark photon; an example matter power spectrum was shown Fig. 2.

We conclude this subsection by noting that we have made a fairly conservative assumption of no coupling with the SM, in order to illustrate a limiting case. In many models of secluded sectors small couplings with the SM may still be present, for example if the mediator VV decays back to SM particles. This can change the NeffN_{\textrm{eff}} prediction, however the SIDM considerations still apply. Indeed, SIDM bounds are also important in the direct coupling scenarios discussed below, as well as in many other dark sector models that don’t fall in the simplistic classification given here.

III.2  Cosmology of direct coupling scenarios

At the other end of dark sector scenarios discussed here, the DM is in thermal equilibrium with the SM plasma throughout freezeout. The DM annihilates into SM particles (or annihilates into particles which decay to SM particles) and the energy density of the dark sector is thus deposited back into the SM thermal bath. This would appear to get around the NeffN_{\textrm{eff}} bounds from BBN and the CMB discussed above, if the DM is sufficiently heavy. However, there are additional effects on BBN abundances and on the CMB which lead to strong constraints.

BBN —- If the thermal freezeout occurs close to the time of BBN (i.e. DM mass is close to the MeV scale), this can modify the predicted abundance via both the baryon-to-photon ratio and NeffN_{\textrm{eff}}. For instance, suppose DM is in equilibrium with the e±e^{\pm} and γ\gamma thermal bath after neutrino decoupling. When the electrons and positrons annihilate away, some of the energy density goes towards heating the DM. This would temporarily reduce the energy density in the photons, and increase the baryon-to-photon ratio η\eta. An increase in η\eta allows more efficient conversion of deuterium into helium, since the fusion rate competes with dissociation from the high energy photons. As a result, the effect of the DM is reduced D and increased 4He. (Meanwhile, an additional source of radiation in NeffN_{\textrm{eff}} primarily affects BBN by changing the expansion rate and thus increasing the relic n/pn/p ratio; this leads to more D and 4He.) Refs. [105, 106, 107] used measurements of abundances and the baryon density to set lower bounds on the DM mass mχ≳1−10m_{\chi}\gtrsim 1-10 MeV, with the specific number depending on the number of degrees of freedom of the candidate. (It is also interesting to note that these bounds apply generally to any MeV-scale particle that was in equilibrium with the SM around the time of BBN, and does not make any assumption about the particle’s relic abundance.)

CMB —- After freezeout, DM annihilation continues all the way through the epoch of recombination, with a rate given by ρDM2​⟨σ​v⟩/(2​mχ2)\rho_{\rm DM}^{2}\langle\sigma v\rangle/(2m_{\chi}^{2}) for Majorana particles. This is a meager rate that barely changes the DM density, but it is a source of energy injection which does affect the CMB. Accounting for the energy released in the annihilation (2​mχ)(2m_{\chi}), the rate of energy deposited per volume and time is parametrized as

d​Ed​V​d​t​(z)=ρc2​Ωcdm2​(1+z)6​⟨σ​v⟩mχ​f​(z)\displaystyle\frac{dE}{dV\,dt}(z)=\rho_{c}^{2}\Omega_{\rm cdm}^{2}(1+z)^{6}\frac{\langle\sigma v\rangle}{m_{\chi}}f(z) (67)

where f⁡(z)f(z) is typically an O⁡(1)O(1) number characterizing the efficiency of energy deposition at redshift zz [110, 111]. For instance, annihilation into photons in a “transparency window” (energies and redshifts where the photon cooling time is relatively slower compared to the expansion rate) or annihilation into neutrinos would reduce the efficiency. The physical effect of the late energy injection is primarily to modify the ionization history: there is an increase in residual ionized hydrogen. CMB photons scatter off the free electrons, leading to damping at small scales in the CMB power spectra (ℓ≳200\ell\gtrsim 200) and an increase in the power for CMB polarization (EE) at large scales (ℓ≲200\ell\lesssim 200) [112].

CMB bounds on DM annihilation are quoted in terms of an effective efficiency fefff_{\rm eff}, which is the leading coefficient when f⁡(z)f(z) is decomposed into a set of basis functions characterized by their effect on the CMB [111]; this approach has been shown to capture most of the effects of DM annihilation [113]. The most recent result from Planck 2018 is [38]

feff​⟨σ​v⟩mχ<2.2×10−26​cm3/s69​GeV\displaystyle f_{\rm eff}\frac{\langle\sigma v\rangle}{m_{\chi}}<\frac{2.2\times 10^{-26}\,{\rm cm}^{3}/{\rm s}}{69\,{\rm GeV}}\, (68)

for ss-wave annihilation. This can be compared with the thermal relic cross section given in Eq. 34. For DM annihilating into SM fermions with the thermal relic cross section, this excludes masses below ∼10−30\sim 10-30 GeV, depending on the final state! Fig. 11 shows the bounds for a range final states in the annihilation. This is thus an important consideration models of light DM. However, these bounds have limited applicability to some classes of models, including asymmetric DM, models with an inelastic splitting so that annihilation is kinematically forbidden at recombination, and those where the DM annihilation is primarily pp-wave (scales as v2v^{2}). The latter two examples utilize the fact that DM is generally extremely cold by the time of recombination.

An one example, consider complex scalar DM ϕ\phi which annihilates through a vector VV into SM fermions. The coupling of the scalar with the vector is given by gϕVμ(iϕ∗∂μϕ+h.c.)g_{\phi}V^{\mu}\left(i\phi^{*}\partial_{\mu}\phi+{\rm h.c.}\right), and we assume an interaction with SM fermions given by gf​Vμ​f¯​γμ​fg_{f}V^{\mu}\bar{f}\gamma_{\mu}f. The amplitude is proportional to the difference in 4-momenta of the initial states, and in limit of non-relativistic DM, this gives a factor of mϕ​vrelm_{\phi}v_{\rm rel} where vrelv_{\rm rel} is the relative velocity of the initial states. The annihilation cross section for vrel≪cv_{\rm rel}\ll c and mf≪mϕm_{f}\ll m_{\phi} is given by

⟨σ​v⟩=σ​vrel=16​π​gϕ2​gf2​mϕ2​vrel2(4​mϕ2−mV2)2+mV2​ΓV2\displaystyle\langle\sigma v\rangle=\sigma v_{\rm rel}=\frac{1}{6\pi}\frac{g_{\phi}^{2}g_{f}^{2}m_{\phi}^{2}v_{\rm rel}^{2}}{(4m_{\phi}^{2}-m_{V}^{2})^{2}+m_{V}^{2}\Gamma_{V}^{2}} (69)

where ΓV\Gamma_{V} is the width of the VV. For further discussion of this benchmark as well the one with an inelastic splitting, see for example Ref. [114].

In addition to the CMB, there are numerous other ways to search for DM annihilation, which are beyond the scope of this discussion. BBN bounds on energy injection from DM annihilation have also been considered [115], and are generally weaker for ss-wave annihilation. Annihilation in the Milky Way is a source of gamma rays and cosmic rays; efforts to detect such signals are described within this lecture series [109].

From the perspective of DM models, the BBN and CMB bounds have the strongest implications. Summarizing Lecture 3 so far, we find:

  • •

    DM candidates below the GeV scale can fall in a few classes, including: secluded, such that there is little or no annihilation to SM particles; asymmetric; and models with pp-wave or kinematic suppression.

  • •

    DM candidates below the MeV scale must be thermally decoupled from the SM thermal bath at the time of BBN and freezeout. (An exception is DM which comes into equilibrium with neutrinos after neutrino decoupling [88].) Sub-MeV models are therefore often secluded or not thermal (see freeze-in discussion in Section II.4.1), and NeffN_{\textrm{eff}} bounds are important.

III.3  Portals with the SM

Having outlined the general features for the cosmology of light DM, we next turn to specific mediators to the SM. In the direct coupling scenario, a mediator interaction with SM states is essential for setting the relic abundance and there is a minimum coupling size needed, which can be translated into a minimal predicted signal in experiments. In the secluded scenario, a mediator-SM interaction can assist in depleting excess energy/entropy and provides a way to search for DM in laboratory experiments, but the signal strength may vary much more.

Commonly studied mediator portals with the SM include:

  • •

    Kinetic mixing portal −- a vector VV has an interaction κ2cosθw​Vμ​ν​Bμ​ν\frac{\kappa}{2\cos\theta_{w}}V_{\mu\nu}B^{\mu\nu} where Bμ​νB^{\mu\nu} is the hypercharge field strength. Since this is a renormalizable operator consistent with SM gauge invariance, we can regard it as an operator that is generically present in the effective field theory. The kinetic mixing is also generated from loops of heavy fermions. After electroweak symmetry breaking, the operator results in a kinetic mixing with the photon κ2​Vμ​ν​Fμ​ν\frac{\kappa}{2}V_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} and VV is typically called a dark photon. (Note the kinetic mixing of a vector with the SM photon is variously called ε\varepsilon, κ\kappa, or χ\chi in the literature. We will stick with the notation κ\kappa here.)

  • •

    Higgs portal −- suppose a scalar mediator ϕ\phi has interactions ϕ2​H†​H\phi^{2}H^{\dagger}H and ϕ​H†​H\phi H^{\dagger}H with the Higgs doublet HH. These interactions can generate a mixing of ϕ\phi with the Higgs boson hh after electroweak symmetry breaking, which in turn leads to couplings of the scalar with SM fermions ∝yf​ϕ​f¯​f\propto y_{f}\phi\bar{f}f. There are also extensions of this with a two-Higgs doublet model (2HDM).

  • •

    Axion portal −- a pseudoscalar (or axion-like particle) aa can have couplings to SM fermions, ∂μafa​f¯​γμ​γ5​f\frac{\partial_{\mu}a}{f_{a}}\bar{f}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{5}f, or to gauge bosons afa​G​G~\frac{a}{f_{a}}G\tilde{G}, afa​F​F~\frac{a}{f_{a}}F\tilde{F}, etc.

  • •

    Neutrino portal −- this refers to the interaction L¯​H​νs\bar{L}H\nu_{s} where LL is a SM lepton doublet and νs\nu_{s} is a sterile neutrino. While sterile neutrinos are considered as DM candidates themselves, they could also serve as a mediator to a dark sector (consisting minimally of an additional dark fermion and scalar that can couple to νs\nu_{s}).

These portals are also the lowest-dimension operators that connect new particles (that are neutral with respect to the SM) to the SM. We next give an overview of some of the constraints and searches for light mediators.

III.3.1  Vector portal

Perhaps the most often studied mediator in recent times is kinetically-mixed dark photon, owing to the appeal of a simple U⁡(1)U(1) extension with a rich phenomenology and the absence of any flavor problems. Focusing on the interactions with just the photon (most relevant for the low-energy phenomenology), the vacuum interactions for this portal are:

ℒ⊃−14​Fμ​ν​Fμ​ν−14​Vμ​ν​Vμ​ν+κ2​Fμ​ν​Vμ​ν+12​mV2​Vμ​Vμ+e​Aμ​JEMμ+gχ​Vμ​JDμ\displaystyle{\cal L}\supset-\frac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{4}V_{\mu\nu}V^{\mu\nu}+\frac{\kappa}{2}F_{\mu\nu}V^{\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{2}m_{V}^{2}V_{\mu}V^{\mu}+eA_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{\rm EM}+g_{\chi}V_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{D} (70)

where JEMμJ^{\mu}_{\rm EM} is the electromagnetic current and JDμJ^{\mu}_{D} is a dark current with gauge coupling gχg_{\chi}. The kinetic mixing parameter κ\kappa can be positive or negative, though constraints are typically shown on the absolute value |κ||\kappa|. In addition, there are the kinetic or mass terms for any dark charged particles, which aren’t written explicitly in order to be general. The vector mass could arise from a dark Higgs mechanism, where the dark Higgs boson is extremely massive and has been integrated out of the theory (i.e, a Stueckelberg mass term). However, in some dark sector models the dark Higgs is also a light degree of freedom and important to the phenomenology.

First consider the case that mV=0m_{V}=0. Then we can make a field redefinition V~μ=Vμ−κ​Aμ\tilde{V}_{\mu}=V_{\mu}-\kappa A_{\mu}. This eliminates the kinetic mixing term, and we are left with the following interactions:

ℒ⊃−14​(1−κ2)​Fμ​ν​Fμ​ν−14​V~μ​ν​V~μ​ν+e​Aμ​JEMμ+gχ​(V~μ+κ​Aμ)​JDμ\displaystyle{\cal L}\supset-\frac{1}{4}(1-\kappa^{2})F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{4}\tilde{V}_{\mu\nu}\tilde{V}^{\mu\nu}+eA_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{\rm EM}+g_{\chi}\left(\tilde{V}_{\mu}+\kappa A_{\mu}\right)J^{\mu}_{D} (71)

where the factor of (1−κ2)(1-\kappa^{2}) in the photon kinetic term can be eliminated by a field (or electric charge) redefinition. In the absence of a dark current JDμJ^{\mu}_{D}, we would have a completely decoupled vector V~\tilde{V} with no observable effects. Hence in the massless vector limit, we expect that the only limits would come from effects that involve the DM. Now suppose there is a DM particle, for example JDμ=χ¯​γμ​χJ^{\mu}_{D}=\bar{\chi}\gamma^{\mu}\chi. In this basis, it is clear that the DM couples to the photon with an effective charge κ​gχ\kappa g_{\chi} or millicharge Q=κ​gχ/eQ=\kappa g_{\chi}/e. This model gives an explicit realization of millicharged DM, discussed earlier in these lectures around Eq. 45.

Now we examine what happens when mV≠0m_{V}\neq 0, starting with the vacuum Lagrangian. Another often-used basis comes from making the field redefinition A~μ=Aμ−κ​Vμ\tilde{A}_{\mu}=A_{\mu}-\kappa V_{\mu}, which eliminates the kinetic mixing term:

ℒ⊃−14​F~μ​ν​F~μ​ν−14​(1−κ2)​Vμ​ν​Vμ​ν+12​mV2​Vμ​Vμ+e⁡(A~μ+κ​Vμ)​JEMμ+gχ​Vμ​JDμ\displaystyle{\cal L}\supset-\frac{1}{4}\tilde{F}_{\mu\nu}\tilde{F}^{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{4}(1-\kappa^{2})V_{\mu\nu}V^{\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{2}m_{V}^{2}V_{\mu}V^{\mu}+e(\tilde{A}_{\mu}+\kappa V_{\mu})J^{\mu}_{\rm EM}+g_{\chi}V_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{D} (72)

where we see that dark photon mass eigenstate VV couples to SM charged particles. Of course, the physics is independent of any field redefinitions or change of basis for the A,VA,V fields77 7 One could also use this basis for the massless mVm_{V} limit. Then in the absence of a dark current, there is no phenomenological difference from regular QED. One can then check that Coulomb scattering, bremsstrahlung etc, are all the same as in QED up to an overall redefinition of electric charge squared as e2​(1+κ2)e^{2}(1+\kappa^{2}) in the limit κ≪1\kappa\ll 1. This redefinition of electric charge is identical to the charge renormalization in the basis of Eq. 71. . This basis is most often used in collider studies of dark photon phenomenology, where the vacuum assumption is valid. However, one must be more careful when considering dark photons in a dense medium, for example in the early universe, in stars, or in a solid state material.

The in-medium Lagrangian for the vector portal must account for the photon dispersion and mass, which leads to modified couplings. In Appendix B, we derive the effective Lagrangian in detail, accounting for the in-medium photon properties. To illustrate why this is relevant for the constraints on a dark photon, consider emission of dark photons in stars. This emission would the stellar luminosity and lifetime, and forms the basis for an important class of constraints on dark photons. The photon dispersion in typical stars has an effective mass given by the plasma frequency ωp≃0.1−10\omega_{p}\simeq 0.1-10 keV. Accounting for in-medium effects, the total emission rate is proportional to (κ​mV/ωp)2(\kappa m_{V}/\omega_{p})^{2} in the limit of mV≪ωpm_{V}\ll\omega_{p} [116]; this would not be the case if we just took the vacuum couplings. (For a derivation of this scaling with mVm_{V}, see Appendix B.)

The stellar constraints on kinetic mixing κ\kappa and dark photon mass mVm_{V} are shown in Fig. 12, where we see the 1/mV1/m_{V} scaling in the bounds labeled ‘solar lifetime’, HB (for horizontal branch stars) and RG (for red giants). The 1/mV1/m_{V} dependence can also be seen in the bounds from emission of dark photons in SN1987a [117]. All of these results assume no coupling to DM, and no other hidden sector states. If there is a large population of DM in the star or if the dark photon decays quickly to DM, this might affect whether the dark photons escape. If there is a sufficiently low mass dark Higgs in the theory, the constraints also dramatically change and the bounds on κ\kappa are independent of mVm_{V} in the low mass limit [116].

For mV≳105m_{V}\gtrsim 10^{5} eV, there are a variety of bounds shown for a visibly-decaying dark photon (i.e. assuming the dark photon does not decay to other dark sector states). In particular, there are accelerator bounds for mV>2​mem_{V}>2m_{e}, where the constraints at κ<10−3\kappa<10^{-3} come from beam dump experiments. There is a vibrant experimental program to search for visibly-decaying and invisibly-decaying dark photons, which aims to cover a significant fraction of open parameter space for MeV <mV<<m_{V}< GeV and κ>10−5\kappa>10^{-5}. We refer the reader to works such as Refs. [79, 131, 132] which more clearly describe the state of the art in accelerator bounds and prospects.

For mV<10−6m_{V}<10^{-6} eV the most important bounds are from resonant conversion of CMB photons into dark photons [120] and from fifth force searches [121]. There are also superradiance bounds on gravitational production of dark photons in the small coupling regime and in the mass ranges 6×10−20​eV<mV<2×10−17​eV6\times 10^{-20}\,\textrm{eV}<m_{V}<2\times 10^{-17}\,\textrm{eV} and 5×10−14​eV<mV<2×10−11​eV5\times 10^{-14}\,\textrm{eV}<m_{V}<2\times 10^{-11}\,\textrm{eV} [133, 134]; they are not shown on the plot as the small coupling regime still needs to precisely quantified. Aside from the superradiance bounds, there are very few limits in the ultralight regime where mV≲10−14m_{V}\lesssim 10^{-14} eV. This is an important feature specific to dark photon phenomenology. As the vector mass goes to zero, emission of dark photons goes to zero due to the in-medium effects discussed above. Meanwhile, searches for fifth forces are also more challenging: traditional searches for fifth forces rely on the large coherent charge of macroscopic objects, which doesn’t apply for the dark photon since most objects are neutral. In the low mass limit, the Compton wavelength of the dark photon is also so large that laboratory searches for modifications to Coulomb’s law are ineffective. Thus ultralight vectors with fairly large kinetic mixing κ\kappa is possible.

Finally, note that we have shown here the most competitive bounds on a general dark photon. A few other results are not shown to keep the plot simpler; some of the other results can be found in the recent summary plot in Ref. [135], for example. If the dark photon itself forms a large fraction of the dark matter, there are additional constraints.

The situation is more difficult for other vector mediators. A gauged B−LB-L is strongly constrained for mV≲m_{V}\lesssim eV by fifth force searches, since in this case a macroscopic neutral material can have a large B−LB-L charge. (Summary plots of the constraints can be found in Refs. [136, 87], for example.) Other anomaly-free combinations of lepton number could also be considered, such as Lμ−LτL_{\mu}-L_{\tau} [137, 138]. Alternatively, it is possible to gauge an anomalous global symmetry such as U​(1)BU(1)_{B}; while this may still be viable in the high mediator mass regime, there are strong constraints for sub-GeV masses (for example, see Refs. [139, 140]). Going beyond pure vector couplings, one could consider a massive vector with axial couplings. However, a massive axial vector is not gauge invariant by itself, and additional ingredients must be supplied in the model; once these are included, there are also severe constraints [141].

As a result, the dark photon remains the most compelling and viable vector mediator, especially for sub-GeV dark sectors where low mass mediators are needed to set the DM relic abundance. When mV>mχm_{V}>m_{\chi}, then direct annihilation of DM DM →e+​e−\to e^{+}e^{-} is sufficient to set the relic abundances. In this direct coupling scenario, DM with mass mχ≳m_{\chi}\gtrsim few MeV is viable given the BBN considerations discussed earlier. If mV<mχm_{V}<m_{\chi}, DM annihilation to mediators is possible; then the DM mass may be as low as the 1-10 keV scale, which is consistent with warm DM and BBN limits as long as the dark sector is decoupled from the SM plasma and sufficiently cold. And in the limit of ultralight mediator mV≪eVm_{V}\ll\textrm{eV}, the DM behaves effectively like a millicharged particle and freeze-in of DM through an ultralight vector is an interesting benchmark. In addition to being instrumental for setting the DM relic abundance, the vector portal is a useful ingredient in models where some heat exchange with the SM sector is needed to dump excess energy/entropy. In the last subsection of this lecture, we will summarize with two specific benchmarks for DM coupled to a dark photon mediator, where the correct relic abundance is obtained.

III.3.2  Scalar mediator portals

A scalar mediator with coupling to SM fermions could arise from the Higgs portal mentioned above, or from other extensions of the SM. Let’s parameterize the interactions as yn​ϕ​n¯​ny_{n}\phi\bar{n}n (where we assume equal coupling to neutrons and protons) and ye​ϕ​e¯​ey_{e}\phi\bar{e}e, where yny_{n} and yey_{e} need not be directly related. The DM also has an interaction yχ​ϕ​χ¯​χy_{\chi}\phi\bar{\chi}\chi.

Fig. 13 shows the allowed parameter space for the interactions, taken from Ref. [87]. The stellar emission constraints discussed for the vector portal are also important for the scalar portals, with the difference that the constraints are independent of the mediator mass for masses below ∼\sim10 keV. (The precise cutoff of the stellar constraints is quite sensitive to the assumed temperatures and plasma frequencies in the stars.) For masses well below 1 eV, fifth force constraints on the new Yukawa interaction start to become the most important bound for nucleon interactions.

The bounds on scalars for mϕ≳m_{\phi}\gtrsim MeV are from accelerator searches. For the ϕ​e¯​e\phi\bar{e}e operator, the results shown assume mϕ<2​mχm_{\phi}<2m_{\chi} so that the mediator decays to visible states. For the yn​ϕ​n¯​ny_{n}\phi\bar{n}n operator, the bounds from rare meson decays B→K​ϕB\to K\phi and K→π​ϕK\to\pi\phi assume the mediator only has a coupling to the gluons; these can differ if the scalar couples to any SM quarks. For example, see Refs. [87, 148] for a scalar which couples to top quarks only or up quarks only. Ref. [149] considered freeze-in (and subsequent decay) of the scalar Higgs portal mediator to set additional bounds, but we don’t show them here as they are specific to the Higgs portal and depend on the reheating scale.

Due to the strong stellar and fifth force constraints, thermal freezeout of DM in the direct coupling scenario is only possible in a limited region of the parameter space shown. Of course, if there are only ϕ​n¯​n\phi\bar{n}n interactions, then sub-GeV DM has no kinematically accessible annihilation channels. If there are ϕ​e¯​e\phi\bar{e}e interactions, then thermal freezeout from χ​χ¯→e+​e−\chi\bar{\chi}\to e^{+}e^{-} (though an off-shell ϕ\phi) is only viable for mχ,mϕ≳10​MeVm_{\chi},m_{\phi}\gtrsim 10\,\textrm{MeV}. Comparing with the right panel of Fig. 13, the coupling yey_{e} can be sufficiently large if we consider the open parameter space above the beam dump and SN constraints. This is also consistent with the BBN bounds discussed earlier.

If mϕ<mχm_{\phi}<m_{\chi}, then thermal freezeout is possible for a larger range of DM masses, as low as the keV scale. Additional hidden sector states are typically needed for thermal freezeout of sub-MeV DM through a scalar mediator [86, 87]. As discussed in Section III.1.1, the self-interacting DM bounds are a strong constraint on the coupling of ϕ\phi with DM, and exclude the couplings yχy_{\chi} where DM annihilation to an ultralight mediator can set the relic abundance. These issues can be resolved if ϕ\phi decays to light hidden sector states or if the relic abundance is set by DM annihilation to other states which don’t mediate DM self-interactions or DM-SM interactions. However, the stellar and fifth force bounds make the prospect of detecting DM which interacts via a sub-MeV scalar mediator quite challenging.

For the scalar Higgs portal mediator specifically, dark sector models are only viable in the mass range mχ≳m_{\chi}\gtrsim MeV and for mϕ<mχm_{\phi}<m_{\chi} [150] (assuming no additional hidden sector states beyond the mediator and DM). Freeze-in of light DM through a Higgs portal mediator is also challenging due to the stellar constraints, and here it was shown that the entire DM relic abundance can be obtained only for DM masses of O⁡(GeV)O(\textrm{GeV}) [151].

III.4  Summary and benchmarks

In this section, we have presented the general constraints and considerations for sub-GeV dark sector model building, summarizing the possibilities for just a few portals. Here we identify some specific models that will motivate our final lectures on direct detection searches. To be concrete, consider the following two benchmarks with the kinetically-mixed vector portal:

  • •

    mχ=10m_{\chi}=10 MeV, mVm_{V} = 30 MeV, gχ=0.3g_{\chi}=0.3 and κ=10−4\kappa=10^{-4} (thermal relic, direct coupling)

  • •

    mχ=1m_{\chi}=1 MeV, mV=10−12m_{V}=10^{-12} eV, gχ=3×10−6g_{\chi}=3\times 10^{-6}, and κ=10−6\kappa=10^{-6} (freeze-in)

where gχg_{\chi} is the coupling of the dark photon with Dirac fermion DM.
