    Exercise: Which type of scattering is mediated by heavy pseudoscalar exchange, where the operator is χ¯​γ5​χ​q¯​γ5​q\bar{\chi}\gamma^{5}\chi\,\bar{q}\gamma^{5}q? Find the nonrelativistic operator, up to O⁡(1)O(1) factors. What about χ¯​γμ​γ5​χ​q¯​γμ​q\bar{\chi}\gamma_{\mu}\gamma^{5}\chi\,\bar{q}\gamma^{\mu}q and χ¯​γμ​χ​q¯​γμ​γ5​q\bar{\chi}\gamma_{\mu}\chi\,\bar{q}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{5}q?

IV.2.1  Heavy scalar exchange

So far, we have dealt with light quark matrix elements in nucleons. What about operators such as Gμ​ν​Gμ​νG^{\mu\nu}G_{\mu\nu} or those involving heavy quarks? We need to consider these matrix elements in order to properly treat the scalar operator CS​mqmh2​v​χ¯​χ​q¯​q\frac{C_{S}m_{q}}{m_{h}^{2}\,v}\bar{\chi}\chi\bar{q}q, with a sum over all quarks for Higgs exchange. Heavy quarks are integrated out at the scale given by the mass of the quark, where integrating out a single flavor generates the loop-induced operator

−CSmh2​v​αs12​π​χ¯​χ​Gμ​ν​Gμ​ν\displaystyle-\frac{C_{S}}{m_{h}^{2}\,v}\,\frac{\alpha_{s}}{12\pi}\bar{\chi}\chi G^{\mu\nu}G_{\mu\nu} (87)

in the effective field theory. The DM coupling is then determined in terms of matrix elements for the light quarks and gluon field strength, given by

⟨n⁡(k′)|mq​q¯​q|n⁡(k)⟩\displaystyle\langle n(k^{\prime})|m_{q}\bar{q}q|n(k)\rangle =mn​fT,qn​u¯n​(k′)​un​(k)\displaystyle=m_{n}f_{T,q}^{n}\,\bar{u}_{n}(k^{\prime})u_{n}(k) (88)
⟨n⁡(k′)|αs​Gμ​ν​Gμ​ν|n⁡(k)⟩\displaystyle\langle n(k^{\prime})|\alpha_{s}G^{\mu\nu}G_{\mu\nu}|n(k)\rangle =−8​π9​mn​fT,gn​u¯n​(k′)​un​(k)\displaystyle=-\frac{8\pi}{9}m_{n}f_{T,g}^{n}\,\bar{u}_{n}(k^{\prime})u_{n}(k) (89)

where the coefficients fT,gn,fT,qnf_{T,g}^{n},f_{T,q}^{n} can be determined through a combination of experimental data and lattice calculations. Recent discussions of the values and their uncertainties can be found in Ref. [175, 174], and we reproduce the results in Table 2.

For the scalar operator, the final matrix element for a given nucleon nn is then given by

ℳ\displaystyle{\cal M} =CSmh2​v​mn​(fT,un+fT,dn+fT,sn+29​fT,gn)​u¯χ​(p′)​uχ​(p)​u¯n​(k′)​un​(k)\displaystyle=\frac{C_{S}}{m_{h}^{2}\,v}m_{n}\left(f_{T,u}^{n}+f_{T,d}^{n}+f_{T,s}^{n}+\frac{2}{9}f_{T,g}^{n}\right)\bar{u}_{\chi}(p^{\prime})u_{\chi}(p)\bar{u}_{n}(k^{\prime})u_{n}(k) (90)
≈4​mχ​mn×CS​mnmh2​v×0.29×χt′†​χt​ξs′†​ξs\displaystyle\approx 4m_{\chi}m_{n}\times\frac{C_{S}\,m_{n}}{m_{h}^{2}\,v}\times 0.29\times\chi_{t^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\chi_{t}\ \xi_{s^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\xi_{s} (91)

where we have included the DM part as well and used the numerical values of the matrix elements. We will use this result below in estimating the typical cross sections for Higgs exchange.

IV.3  Nuclear recoils from DM scattering

The next step in computing the scattering rate is to turn the nucleon-level matrix elements into matrix elements for DM-nucleus scattering in specific targets. The matrix element of the nucleon level operators with the nucleus state is encapsulated in nuclear form factors. For example,

|⟨N|𝐒n​(q)|N⟩|2\displaystyle|\langle N|{\bf S}_{n}(q)|N\rangle|^{2} =Fspin2​(q)\displaystyle=F^{2}_{\rm spin}(q) (92)
|⟨N|n¯​n|N⟩|2\displaystyle|\langle N|\bar{n}n|N\rangle|^{2} =Fmass2​(q)\displaystyle=F^{2}_{\rm mass}(q) (93)

where again we just take the leading behavior of the matrix element. Computing these form factors requires a model of the bound nucleons inside a nucleus, and therefore involves complicated many-body physics88 8 Similarly, when approaching direct detection of light DM, one needs to account for many-body effects that give rise to the electron and phonon excitations in a material. For instance, we will take a similar approach is defining phonon form factors in L5, except that we sum over all the “bound state” nuclei in a crystal lattice.. A commonly used model is the shell model of nuclei. Let us consider just the scalar n¯​n\bar{n}n operator: in the non-relativistic limit, this is the number density operator for nucleons. The mass form factor can then be written as

F(q)=∫d3𝐱e−i𝐪⋅𝐱ρn​(𝐱)mn\displaystyle F(q)=\int d^{3}{\bf x}\,e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf x}}\ \frac{\rho_{n}({\bf x})}{m_{n}} (94)
→Awhenq→0\displaystyle\to A\quad\text{when}\quad q\to 0 (95)

where ρn​(𝐱)\rho_{n}({\bf x}) is the mass density of nucleons in the nucleus. A commonly used form factor is the Helm form factor [176] since it has a simple analytic expression, F(q)=3​j1​(q​rn)q​rne−(qs)2/2F(q)=\tfrac{3j_{1}(qr_{n})}{qr_{n}}e^{-(qs)^{2}/2}, where j1j_{1} is the first spherical Bessel function and an approximate fit for heavy nuclei can be obtained with rn≈1.14​A1/3r_{n}\approx 1.14A^{1/3} fm and s≈0.9s\approx 0.9 fm. Fig. 15 shows example form factors for various target materials used in experiments. A standard reference with a clear explanation of the spin form factors can be found in Ref. [177].

We now embark on a calculation of the spin-independent scattering rate. For the vector operator, we start with the matrix element in Eq. 83. Squaring, taking the trace, and averaging over final state spins gives

|ℳ|2=(3​CVmZ2)2×(4​mχ​mn)2≡bn2​(4​mχ​mn)2\displaystyle|{\cal M}|^{2}=\left(\frac{3C_{V}}{m_{Z}^{2}}\right)^{2}\times(4m_{\chi}m_{n})^{2}\equiv b_{n}^{2}\,(4m_{\chi}m_{n})^{2} (96)

where we have assumed spin 1/2 fermions as above. The second equality defines bnb_{n}, the DM-nucleon vector coupling. We first determine the cross section for DM-nucleon scattering, where there is no nuclear form factor. Taking the nonrelativistic limit and assuming the initial nucleon is at rest, the differential cross section is given by

d​σn\displaystyle d\sigma_{n} =|ℳ|24​mχ​mn​v​d3​𝐩′(2​π)3​2​mχ​d3​𝐪(2​π)3​2​mn​(2​π)4​δ(4)​(p+k−p′−k′)\displaystyle=\frac{|{\cal M}|^{2}}{4m_{\chi}m_{n}v}\frac{d^{3}{\bf p}^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}2m_{\chi}}\frac{d^{3}{\bf q}}{(2\pi)^{3}2m_{n}}(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{(4)}\left(p+k-p^{\prime}-k^{\prime}\right) (97)
=bn24​π​v2​d​|𝐪|2​d​cos⁡θ​δ​(cos⁡θ−|𝐪|2​μχ​n​v)\displaystyle=\frac{b_{n}^{2}}{4\pi\,v^{2}}d|{\bf q}|^{2}\,d\cos\theta\,\delta\left(\cos\theta-\frac{|{\bf q}|}{2\mu_{\chi n}v}\right) (98)

where vv is the initial DM velocity, cos⁡θ=𝐪^⋅𝐩^\cos\theta=\hat{\bf q}\cdot\hat{\bf p}, and μχ​n\mu_{\chi n} is the reduced mass of the DM and nucleon. Integrating over all kinematically allowed |𝐪|≤2​μχ​n​v|{\bf q}|\leq 2\mu_{\chi n}v, the total cross section is

σn=μχ​n2​bn2π.\displaystyle\sigma_{n}=\frac{\mu_{\chi n}^{2}\,b_{n}^{2}}{\pi}\,. (99)

The differential cross section above can now be generalized to DM-nucleus scattering, where we use NN for nuclear quantities. Using the fact that d​|𝐪|2=2​mN​d​ERd|{\bf q}|^{2}=2m_{N}dE_{R} with ERE_{R} the nuclear recoil energy and including the nuclear form factor, we obtain:

d​σNd​ER\displaystyle\frac{d\sigma_{N}}{dE_{R}} =|ℳ|2π​mN2​v2​F2​(q)​d​cos⁡θ​δ​(cos⁡θ−|𝐪|2​μχ​N​v)\displaystyle=\frac{|{\cal M}|^{2}}{\pi}\frac{m_{N}}{2v^{2}}\,F^{2}(q)\,d\cos\theta\,\delta\left(\cos\theta-\frac{|{\bf q}|}{2\mu_{\chi N}v}\right) (100)
=σnμχ​n2​mN2​v2​F2​(q)​Θ​(v−mN​ER2​μχ​N2)\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{n}}{\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}\frac{m_{N}}{2v^{2}}\,F^{2}(q)\,\Theta\left(v-\sqrt{\frac{m_{N}E_{R}}{2\mu_{\chi N}^{2}}}\right) (101)

In the second line, we have replaced the matrix element squared with the single nucleon cross section. The step function enforces the minimum incoming DM velocity for a recoil of energy ERE_{R}.

The differential rate per unit target mass and per unit time is defined as

d​Rd​ER=NT​nχ​∫d​σd​ER​v​f​(𝐯)​d3​𝐯\displaystyle\frac{dR}{dE_{R}}=N_{T}n_{\chi}\int\frac{d\sigma}{dE_{R}}vf({\bf v})\,d^{3}{\bf v} (102)

with NTN_{T} is the number of nuclei per unit target mass, nχ=ρχ/mχn_{\chi}=\rho_{\chi}/m_{\chi} is the DM number density, and f⁡(𝐯)f(\bf v) is the DM velocity distribution in the lab frame and normalized to unity. Extracting just the dependence on the DM velocity, we can define an integral

g⁡(vmin)≡∫d3​𝐯​f⁡(𝐯)v​Θ​(v−mN​ER2​μχ​N2)\displaystyle g(v_{\rm min})\equiv\int d^{3}{\bf v}\,\frac{f({\bf v})}{v}\Theta\left(v-\sqrt{\frac{m_{N}E_{R}}{2\mu_{\chi N}^{2}}}\right) (103)

with vmin=mN​ER/2​μχ​N2v_{\rm min}=\sqrt{m_{N}E_{R}/2\mu_{\chi N}^{2}}. Finally, we account for the fact that the DM may have different couplings to protons or neutrons and rescale the total rate to obtain:

d​Rd​ER=NT​ρχmχ​σn​mN2​μχ​n2​(bp​Z+bn​(A−Z)bn​A)2​F2​(q)​g​(vmin)\displaystyle\boxed{\frac{dR}{dE_{R}}=N_{T}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\sigma_{n}m_{N}}{2\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}\left(\frac{b_{p}Z+b_{n}(A-Z)}{b_{n}A}\right)^{2}F^{2}(q)\,g(v_{\rm min})}\, (104)

where in this formula bnb_{n} is the neutron coupling and bpb_{p} is the proton coupling.

Similar results can be obtained for axial-vector coupling and heavy scalar exchange. Summing over spins and averaging over initial spin, the cross section for spin-dependent scattering for spin-1/21/2 Dirac fermion DM is given by

σn=3​μχ​n2π​(∑qΔqn​CAmZ2)2≡3​μχ​n2π​(∑qΔqn​dq)2.\displaystyle\sigma_{n}=\frac{3\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}{\pi}\left(\sum_{q}\Delta^{n}_{q}\frac{C_{A}}{m_{Z}^{2}}\right)^{2}\equiv\frac{3\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}{\pi}\left(\sum_{q}\Delta^{n}_{q}d_{q}\right)^{2}. (105)

For a detailed discussion of cross sections and rates for spin-dependent interactions, see Ref. [178]. For heavy scalar exchange, the calculation proceeds in a similar way with

σn=μχ​n2π​(0.29×CS​mnmh2​v)2≡μχ​n2​fn2π.\displaystyle\sigma_{n}=\frac{\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}{\pi}\left(\frac{0.29\times C_{S}m_{n}}{m_{h}^{2}v}\right)^{2}\equiv\frac{\mu_{\chi n}^{2}f_{n}^{2}}{\pi}. (106)

We have given the mapping to commonly used notation in these equations.

We’ve almost gotten most of the relevant formulae down. Before looking at the total scattering rate, we first discuss the DM velocity distribution and g⁡(vmin)g(v_{\rm min}).

IV.3.1  Astrophysics of direct detection

The properties of DM in the solar neighborhood enter in the local DM density ρχ\rho_{\chi} and the velocity distribution f⁡(𝐯)f({\bf v}) of DM particles incident on a target. The local DM density is usually assumed to be ρχ=0.4\rho_{\chi}=0.4 GeV/cm3. This is determined from models of the local gravitational potential (usually within 1 kpc), and different methods lead to variations on this value at the level of 10−50%10-50\%. For a summary of measurements and methods, see Ref. [179].

The DM velocity distribution is more challenging to determine, and this is complicated by the fact that small changes in the velocity distribution can have a large impact on direct detection rates. A simple analytic approximation for the DM velocity distribution is that of a truncated Maxwellian distribution, since we expect the DM in the solar neighborhood to be mostly virialized. In the frame of the Galaxy, this velocity distribution is isotropic with the form:

fGalaxy​(𝐯)=1N⁡(v0)​exp⁡(−𝐯2v02)​Θ​(vesc−|𝐯|)\displaystyle f_{\rm Galaxy}({\bf v})=\frac{1}{N(v_{0})}\exp\left(-\frac{{\bf v}^{2}}{v_{0}^{2}}\right)\Theta(v_{\rm esc}-|{\bf v}|) (107)

where it is usually assumed that v0≈220v_{0}\approx 220 km/s. The distribution is cut off at the local escape speed vescv_{\rm esc}, with estimated values around 500-600 km/s [180, 181]. N⁡(v0)N(v_{0}) is normalization factor such that f⁡(𝐯)f({\bf v}) integrates to unity,

N⁡(v0)=π3/2​v03​[erf⁡(vescv0)−2π​vescv0​exp⁡(−vesc2v02)].\displaystyle N(v_{0})=\pi^{3/2}v_{0}^{3}\left[{\rm erf}\left(\tfrac{v_{\rm esc}}{v_{0}}\right)-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\tfrac{v_{\rm esc}}{v_{0}}\exp\left(-\tfrac{v_{\rm esc}^{2}}{v_{0}^{2}}\right)\right]. (108)

This is known as the Standard Halo Model. One must then boost this to the Earth (lab) frame

fEarth​(𝐯)=1N⁡(v0)​exp⁡(−(𝐯+𝐕e​(t))2v02)​Θ​(ve​s​c−|𝐯+𝐕e​(t)|)\displaystyle f_{\rm Earth}({\bf v})=\frac{1}{N(v_{0})}\exp\left(-\frac{({\bf v}+{\bf V}_{e}(t))^{2}}{v_{0}^{2}}\right)\Theta(v_{esc}-|{\bf v}+{\bf V}_{e}(t)|) (109)

where we can decompose the Earth’s motion into the Sun’s motion in the Galaxy (𝐕⊙{\bf V}_{\rm\odot}) and the orbit of the Earth about the Sun (𝐕⊕{\bf V}_{\rm\oplus}):

𝐕e​(t)=𝐕⊙+𝐕⊕​(t)\displaystyle{\bf V}_{e}(t)={\bf V}_{\rm\odot}+{\bf V}_{\rm\oplus}(t) (110)

For calculating rates, we often neglect the orbital motion of the Earth since |𝐕⊕|≈29.8|{\bf V}_{\rm\oplus}|\approx 29.8 km/s, which is much less than the rotational speed of the Sun |𝐕⊙|≈240|{\bf V}_{\rm\odot}|\approx 240 km/s. The Sun’s motion corresponds to a fixed direction with respect to the Milky Way (in the direction of the constellation Cygnus) and the DM velocity distribution appears to be coming at us from −𝐕⊙-{\bf V}_{\odot}, on average; we therefore often say that there is a DM “wind” coming from Cygnus, although of course there is a distribution in the incoming DM direction. The time-dependence in 𝐕⊕​(t){\bf V}_{\rm\oplus}(t) leads to an additional interesting effect: an annual modulation of the rate as the Earth rotates about the Sun. For a recent review of modulation signals and the astrophysics of direct detection, see Ref. [182].

As defined in Eq. 103, g⁡(vmin)g(v_{\rm min}) is the expectation value of 1/v1/v subject to the minimum energy threshold or velocity threshold. Using the velocity distribution given here with vesc=550v_{\rm esc}=550 km/s, ve=240v_{e}=240 km/s and v0=220v_{0}=220 km/s, we show in Fig. 16 the resulting g⁡(vmin)g(v_{\rm min}). A given experiment uses a particular target nucleus and has an energy threshold, which means that the experiment is sensitive to particular ranges in the DM velocity distribution. Concentrating on the exponential tail, which gives the highest energy recoils, we can approximate g⁡(vmin)g(v_{\rm min}) by

g⁡(vmin)\displaystyle g(v_{\rm min}) ∝∫vminvmaxd​v​v​exp⁡(−v2v02)\displaystyle\propto\int_{v_{\rm min}}^{v_{\rm max}}dv\,v\,\exp\left(-\frac{v^{2}}{v_{0}^{2}}\right) (111)
∝exp⁡(−vmin2v02)−exp⁡(−vmax2v02)≃exp⁡(−mN​ER2​μχ​N2​v02)\displaystyle\propto\exp\left(-\frac{v_{\rm min}^{2}}{v_{0}^{2}}\right)-\exp\left(-\frac{v_{\rm max}^{2}}{v_{0}^{2}}\right)\simeq\exp\left(-\frac{m_{N}E_{R}}{2\mu_{\chi N}^{2}v_{0}^{2}}\right) (112)

where the maximum possible velocity in the lab frame is given by vmax=vesc+vev_{\rm max}=v_{\rm esc}+v_{e} and we have used vmin=mN​ER/2​μχ​N2v_{\rm min}=\sqrt{m_{N}E_{R}/2\mu_{\chi N}^{2}} in the last equality. Thus the minimum velocity threshold for a given recoil energy leads to an exponential drop in ERE_{R} for the differential scattering rate, which can be seen in the right panel of Fig. 16. The typical recoil energy is thus given by ERtypical=2​μχ​N2​v02/mNE_{R}^{\rm typical}=2\mu_{\chi N}^{2}v_{0}^{2}/m_{N}, while the maximum recoil energy is ERmax=2​μχ​N2​(vesc+ve)2/mNE_{R}^{\rm max}=2\mu_{\chi N}^{2}(v_{\rm esc}+v_{e})^{2}/m_{N}.

Of course, the statements above assume that the tail of the DM velocity distribution is well-described by a Maxwellian. It is well known that the simple analytic result above is not a good approximation to more realistic DM velocity distributions from simulations [183, 184, 185]. It is likely that the true distribution is anisotropic within the Galaxy, that there are unvirialized components, and that the hard cutoff at vescv_{\rm esc} is certainly unphysical. In calculating elastic scattering rates for heavier DM, this affects the recoil spectrum and also has a modest effect on the total rates. The impact is larger for low mass DM, where an experiment is usually sensitive only to DM with the highest speeds, and thus we require knowledge of the tail of the distribution. While we do not have a direct measurement of the velocity distribution, recent work has studied the velocity distribution of the metal-poor stellar halo as a proxy for the DM [186, 187, 188]. This gives an empirical way to approximate the DM velocity distribution, and we expect our knowledge to improve with more data.

IV.4  Scattering rates and experimental status

Finally, we can look at typical recoil spectra and the implication of direct detection constraints on DM models. Fig. 17 shows the recoil spectra for a xenon target and typical DM masses that can be constrained by liquid xenon experiments. The exponential suppression derived above in Eq. 112 can be seen, with most of the signal occurring at low recoil energies. Direct detection experiments thus stand to gain significantly in signal rate with reduced thresholds. Particularly for low mass DM mχ≪mNm_{\chi}\ll m_{N}, the reduced mass μχ​N≈mχ\mu_{\chi N}\approx m_{\chi} and the minimum velocity scales as vmin≈mN​ER/(2​mχ2)v_{\rm min}\approx\sqrt{m_{N}E_{R}/(2m_{\chi}^{2})}. This results in a steep drop in the rate for low mass DM. Meanwhile, the minimum velocity for mχ≫mNm_{\chi}\gg m_{N} is vmin≈ER/(2​mN)v_{\rm min}\approx\sqrt{E_{R}/(2m_{N})}, so that the recoil spectra are independent of the DM mass in this limit.

The spectrum shown assumes a spin-independent cross section σn=10−40\sigma_{n}=10^{-40} cm2. This is totally excluded by direct detection experiments for masses in the 10 GeV – 10510^{5} TeV range. Fig. 18 shows the landscape of existing constraints for spin-independent scattering. The current strongest limits are from the XENON1T collaboration [189], with an exposure of almost 10610^{6} kg-day. In the next decade, the sensitivity will improve by another 1-2 orders of magnitude (from experiments such as DarkSide, PandaX, LZ, XENONnT). The sensitivity at low mχm_{\chi} drops rapidly due to the energy thresholds in the experiments, ERth≳5−10E_{R}^{\rm th}\gtrsim 5-10 keV. The sensitivity at high mχm_{\chi} drops because the number density of DM drops as 1/mχ1/m_{\chi}. The constraints on spin-dependent cross sections are weaker, and at the level of 10−4110^{-41} cm2 for coupling to neutron spin and 10−4010^{-40} cm2 for coupling to proton spin (see for example Ref. [190]).

What are the implications for models of WIMPs? Using Eq. 99 and setting CV=gw2∼0.1C_{V}=g_{w}^{2}\sim 0.1 where gwg_{w} is a weak gauge coupling, the typical cross section for a 100 GeV DM candidate scattering through a vector coupling to the ZZ-boson is

σnV≃10−37​cm2.\displaystyle\sigma_{n}^{V}\simeq 10^{-37}\,{\rm cm}^{2}\ . (113)

For Higgs exchange, using Eq. 106 and setting CS=0.01C_{S}=0.01,

σnS≃6×10−47​cm2.\displaystyle\sigma_{n}^{S}\simeq 6\times 10^{-47}\,{\rm cm}^{2}\ . (114)

For some DM candidates (such as Majorana fermion DM), scattering through the vector coupling to the ZZ boson is highly suppressed or zero. For ZZ-exchange and an axial vector coupling with CA=0.1C_{A}=0.1, we use Eq. 105 and obtain

σnA≃6×10−38​cm2.\displaystyle\sigma_{n}^{A}\simeq 6\times 10^{-38}\,{\rm cm}^{2}\ . (115)

We see that ZZ exchange with O⁡(1)O(1) gauge couplings is strongly excluded, and Higgs exchange with couplings CS=0.01−0.1C_{S}=0.01-0.1 are being probed in tonne-scale experiments. (Searches for Higgs invisible decays at the LHC provide a complementary constraint on CSC_{S} if mχ<mh/2m_{\chi}<m_{h}/2, where currently the bounds are comparable for mχ∼m_{\chi}\sim 10 GeV [175, 195, 196].) Of course, it is possible to simply lower the couplings to get around the direct detection bounds. The difficulty with this approach is that the annihilation cross sections become correspondingly weaker as well, meaning it is difficult to obtain the relic abundance by thermal freezeout. This makes the simplest WIMP story more and more difficult to achieve. There are important exceptions, including the case of a pseudo-Dirac electroweak doublet fermion. This is also known as a Higgsino, and the thermal relic can be obtained when the mass is about 1.1 TeV. The lightest neutral fermion in the doublet is a good DM candidate, and it does not have diagonal couplings to the ZZ boson at tree level (which would allow for elastic scattering). The predicted cross section for spin-independent scattering is σn≲10−48\sigma_{n}\lesssim 10^{-48} cm2 due to a cancellation between different contributions [197]. This candidate is extremely challenging to search for in direct detection, indirect detection, and collider experiments. Thus, there are some WIMP candidates that will remain viable for a time to come (see also Refs. [49, 50, 198]).

There are a number of compelling reasons to go beyond nuclear recoils in the 10–100 GeV regime. First, the current approach rapidly loses sensitivity to low mass DM. As we saw, there are many candidates in the sub-GeV regime which reproduce some of the successes for weak-scale candidates. Furthermore, thermal freezeout for light DM requires the presence of addition of new light mediators. If the mediators are sufficiently light, this further modifies the recoil spectrum to favor lower energy recoils. The factors of 1/mZ21/m_{Z}^{2} become replaced with 1/(q2−mV2)≃1/(2​mN​ER)1/(q^{2}-m_{V}^{2})\simeq 1/(2m_{N}E_{R}) for mV≪|𝐪|m_{V}\ll|{\bf q}|. Direct detection with lower thresholds opens up the possibility of exploring new classes of low mass candidates. We turn to the methods and proposals for low-threshold detection next.

V  New directions in direct detection

As highlighted in the previous lecture, conventional direct detection via nuclear recoils becomes much less effective for sub-GeV dark matter due to the much smaller recoil energies. Furthermore, we motivated the presence of light mediators for sub-GeV dark matter, which can further shift the recoil spectra to lower energies.

Direct detection of sub-GeV dark sectors thus requires a different approach, both theoretically and experimentally. An important difference on the theoretical side is the necessity of incorporating many-body physics. Our idealized picture of a free, nearly-at-rest particle just waiting for an incident DM particle to provide some excitement is hardly reflective of reality. Dark matter direct detection requires significant target mass, and typical targets are liquids or solid state materials. Nuclei and electrons in such materials have enormous interactions with each other! The typical inter-atomic spacing in a material is given by ∼\simÅ∼1\sim 1/keV, and similarly, the size of an atom is also given by ∼\simÅ. For scattering of WIMPs, where the momentum transfer may be as large as |𝐪|∼mχ​v≳|{\bf q}|\sim m_{\chi}v\gtrsim MeV, such “condensed matter” effects are usually neglected – but remember that they can still be quite important for experimental detection, and that many-body effects played a role in the nuclear form factors. For light DM, the momentum transfer can be on the keV scale or less, and inter-atom interactions can play an important role in the DM interaction.

In this lecture, we will provide an introduction to the theoretical tools used in some proposed detection scenarios. This is a field that is quickly developing, and there will be no attempt to give a complete review. For a recent white paper that provides more details on experimental status, see Ref. [79]. Rather, the discussion here will center on toy models to provide intuition for the relevant many-body physics. Fig. 19 illustrates the kinematics of DM scattering on free nuclei, as compared with electron scattering or phonon scattering. One of the goals of this lecture will be to understand this figure, and why these alternate scattering modes allow for more of the DM kinetic energy to be deposited in a scattering. Note that we will use the term ‘nuclear recoil’ (NR) as shorthand for scattering off free nuclei at rest, even though phonon scattering is also sensitive to DM that couples dominantly to nuclei.

V.1  Electron recoils

Compared to nuclear recoils, the most important features of electron scattering are that the electron is much lighter than the proton, and its velocity in a typical material is much faster than the DM velocity. Consider an atomic target: the electron is in a bound state with a typical wavefunction size of RBohr=1/(α​me)R_{\rm Bohr}=1/(\alpha m_{e}). The typical momentum of this electron is therefore ke≃1/RBohr=α​mek_{e}\simeq 1/R_{\rm Bohr}=\alpha m_{e} and its velocity ve≃αv_{e}\simeq\alpha. This electron is in an energy eigenstate but not in a momentum eigenstate, and computing scattering requires knowledge of the specific wavefunctions in the material. Before we describe the form factors needed to account for these wavefunctions below, let us repeat the exercise of DM scattering kinematics for free electrons.

As before, the energy deposited ω\omega in a DM scattering is

ω=𝐩⋅𝐪mχ−𝐪22​mχ=Ee​(𝐤′)−Ee​(𝐤),\displaystyle\omega=\frac{{\bf p}\cdot{\bf q}}{m_{\chi}}-\frac{{\bf q}^{2}}{2m_{\chi}}=E_{e}({\bf k}^{\prime})-E_{e}({\bf k}), (116)

but now Ee​(𝐤′)E_{e}({\bf k}^{\prime}) is an in-medium energy eigenvalue. 𝐪=𝐩−𝐩′{\bf q}={\bf p}-{\bf p}^{\prime} is again the momentum transfer. As a toy model, we will just consider the situation of scattering off a free electron with initial velocity ve,i=αv_{e,i}=\alpha. Then energy conservation gives the condition:

𝐩⋅𝐪mχ=𝐤⋅𝐪me−𝐪22​μχ​e,\displaystyle\frac{{\bf p}\cdot{\bf q}}{m_{\chi}}=\frac{{\bf k}\cdot{\bf q}}{m_{e}}-\frac{{\bf q}^{2}}{2\mu_{\chi e}}, (117)

where μχ​e\mu_{\chi e} is the DM-electron reduced mass. Since the electron velocity is much larger than the DM velocity, ve,i=|𝐤|/me≫vχ,i=|𝐩|/mχv_{e,i}=|{\bf k}|/m_{e}\gg v_{\chi,i}=|{\bf p}|/m_{\chi}, let us start by dropping the left-hand-side of the equation above, and estimating the momentum transfer as |𝐪|≃μχ​e​ve,i|{\bf q}|\simeq\mu_{\chi e}v_{e,i}. We can then estimate the recoil energies in two different DM mass regimes:

  • •

    mχ≳mem_{\chi}\gtrsim m_{e}: for heavier DM, the momentum transfer is approximated by |𝐪|≃me​ve,i|{\bf q}|\simeq m_{e}v_{e,i}. This is the expected result for an electron that recoils off a heavy particle. Then the deposited energy using Eq. 116 is

    ω≃me​ve,i​vχ,i≈few eV,\displaystyle\omega\simeq m_{e}v_{e,i}v_{\chi,i}\approx\ \textrm{few eV}, (118)

    approximately independent of mχm_{\chi}. It is worth emphasizing that this is just a typical energy deposition: high ω\omega is possible in a given material, such as for ionization of atoms in Xe (ω>12\omega>12 eV).

  • •

    mχ≲mem_{\chi}\lesssim m_{e}: if we were to use the result |𝐪|≃μχ​e​ve,i≈mχ​ve,i|{\bf q}|\simeq\mu_{\chi e}v_{e,i}\approx m_{\chi}v_{e,i}, we would actually find in Eq. 116 that the energy deposited is negative. The momentum transfer must be bounded from above by |𝐪|≃mχ​vχ,i|{\bf q}|\simeq m_{\chi}v_{\chi,i} for a positive ω\omega: this effectively tells us that the final state phase space becomes much more restricted. Again, this is the expected result in the limit of a light DM particle scattering off the much more massive electron. The allowed energy deposition is

    ω≃12​mχ​vχ,i2,\displaystyle\omega\simeq\frac{1}{2}m_{\chi}v_{\chi,i}^{2}, (119)

    meaning potentially all of the DM kinetic energy can be deposited.

These arguments are translated schematically into the red curve in Fig. 19, which shows the typical electron recoil energy as a function of DM mass. Of course, electrons are not actually free in the targets, nor are they in momentum eigenstates, so that arbitrarily high electron velocities are possible (though with suppressed probability). In the remainder of this subsection, we work out the scattering rate explicitly.

As a simple calculation where the result can be obtained analytically, we will consider ionization of a Hydrogen atom from DM-electron scattering. We will take the outgoing states to consist of free electrons; technically, the outgoing electron wavefunction experiences a distortion in the vicinity of the nucleus, but we will neglect this correction for the moment. The scattering cross section can be written as [199, 200]

(σ​v)j=∫d3​𝐩′(2​π)3​d3​𝐤′(2​π)3​(2​π)​δ​(Δ​Ee−ω)​|ℳfree|216​mχ2​me2​|fj→𝐤′​(𝐪)|2\displaystyle(\sigma v)_{j}=\int\frac{d^{3}{\bf p}^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{d^{3}{\bf k}^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,(2\pi)\delta(\Delta E_{e}-\omega)\,\frac{|{\cal M}_{\rm free}|^{2}}{16m_{\chi}^{2}m_{e}^{2}}\,|f_{j\to{\bf k}^{\prime}}({\bf q})|^{2} (120)

with |ℳfree|2|{\cal M}_{\rm free}|^{2} is the matrix element squared for scattering off a free electron (e.g. Eq. 74). The index jj labels a possible initial state, while the outgoing states are labelled by a wavevector 𝐤′{\bf k}^{\prime}. (As before, 𝐩′{\bf p}^{\prime} is the outgoing DM momentum.) The form factor accounts for the wavefunctions of initial and final electron states, and is given by

fj→𝐤′​(𝐪)=V​∫d3​𝐫​ψj​(𝐫)​ψ𝐤′∗​(𝐫)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫,\displaystyle f_{j\to{\bf k}^{\prime}}({\bf q})=\sqrt{V}\int d^{3}{\bf r}\ \psi_{j}({\bf r})\,\psi_{{\bf k}^{\prime}}^{*}({\bf r})\,e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}}, (121)

where VV is a volume to account for wavefunction normalization, to be explained below. We are not used to seeing volume factors in our conventional QFT calculations, but including them will be extremely helpful in matching up with quantum mechanics conventions (used more often in other parts of physics!).

Before diving into a calculation for bound electrons, we first use the above result for scattering off free electrons at rest.

V.1.1  Free electron cross section

For free electrons, we can use initial and final plane-wave wavefunctions. Then the above result reproduces the expectation for scattering of free particles:

|fj→𝐤′​(𝐪)|2\displaystyle|f_{j\to{\bf k}^{\prime}}({\bf q})|^{2} =|V​∫d3​𝐫​ei​𝐤⋅𝐫V​e−i𝐤′⋅𝐫V​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫|2\displaystyle=\left|\sqrt{V}\int d^{3}{\bf r}\,\frac{e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf r}}}{\sqrt{V}}\,\frac{e^{-i{\bf k}^{\prime}\cdot{\bf r}}}{\sqrt{V}}\,e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}}\right|^{2} (122)
=[(2​π)3​δ(3)​(𝐤+𝐪−𝐤′)]2/V\displaystyle=\left[(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{(3)}\left({\bf k}+{\bf q}-{\bf k}^{\prime}\right)\right]^{2}/V (123)
=(2​π)3​δ(3)​(𝐤+𝐪−𝐤′)\displaystyle=(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{(3)}\left({\bf k}+{\bf q}-{\bf k}^{\prime}\right) (124)

where we have included the normalization of the wavefunctions in terms of the volume factor VV, and take the large volume limit in the end. We have also used that the (2​π)3​δ(3)​(𝟎)/V→1(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{(3)}({\bf 0})/V\rightarrow 1 for a momentum-space delta function. This reproduces the standard free particle scattering cross section.

For scattering via the dark photon mediator for instance, the spin-averaged matrix element is (see definitions and discussion around Eq. 74):

|ℳ|2=16​gχ2​κ2​e2​mχ2​me2((qμ2)−mV2)2≈16​gχ2​κ2​e2​mχ2​me2(|𝐪|2+mV2)2.\displaystyle|{\cal M}|^{2}=\frac{16g_{\chi}^{2}\kappa^{2}e^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}m_{e}^{2}}{((q_{\mu}^{2})-m_{V}^{2})^{2}}\approx\frac{16g_{\chi}^{2}\kappa^{2}e^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}m_{e}^{2}}{(|{\bf q}|^{2}+m_{V}^{2})^{2}}. (125)

Here we used that for scattering of non-relativistic particles, q0≪|𝐪|q^{0}\ll|{\bf q}|. We will rewrite the matrix element in terms of an average cross section times DM form factor:

μχ​e2​|ℳ|216​π​mχ2​me2≡σ¯e​FDM2​(q),FDM2​(q)≡((α​me)2+mV2|𝐪|2+mV2)2\displaystyle\frac{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}|{\cal M}|^{2}}{16\pi m_{\chi}^{2}m_{e}^{2}}\equiv\bar{\sigma}_{e}F_{\rm DM}^{2}(q),\ \ \ F^{2}_{\rm DM}(q)\equiv\left(\frac{(\alpha m_{e})^{2}+m_{V}^{2}}{|{\bf q}|^{2}+m_{V}^{2}}\right)^{2} (126)

where FDM2​(q)F^{2}_{\rm DM}(q) absorbs the qq-dependence of the matrix element.

For initial electrons at rest (k=0)(k=0), the final electron has energy ER=q2/(2​me)E_{R}=q^{2}/(2m_{e}) and the cross section is then given by

σ​v\displaystyle\sigma v =σ¯eμχ​e2​∫d3​𝐪4​π​δ​(q22​μχ​e−p​q​cos⁡θmχ)​FDM2​(q)\displaystyle=\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{e}}{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int\frac{d^{3}{\bf q}}{4\pi}\,\delta\left(\tfrac{q^{2}}{2\mu_{\chi e}}-\tfrac{pq\cos\theta}{m_{\chi}}\right)\,F_{\rm DM}^{2}(q) (127)
=σ¯eμχ​e2​∫d​ln⁡ER​ER​me2​v​θ​(v−q2​μχ​e)​FDM2​(q)\displaystyle=\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{e}}{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int d\ln E_{R}\frac{E_{R}m_{e}}{2v}\,\theta\left(v-\tfrac{q}{2\mu_{\chi e}}\right)\,F_{\rm DM}^{2}(q) (128)

where we first changed variables d3​𝐩′=d3​𝐪d^{3}{\bf p}^{\prime}=d^{3}{\bf q} and then q​d​q=d​ER​meq\,dq=dE_{R}m_{e}. The initial relative velocity is just p/mχp/m_{\chi} in this case. We can write the above as

σ=σ¯e​∫ERmaxd​ERERmax​FDM2​(q),\displaystyle\sigma=\bar{\sigma}_{e}\int^{E_{R}^{\rm max}}\frac{dE_{R}}{E_{R}^{\rm max}}\,F_{\rm DM}^{2}(q)\ , (129)

which is similar to the result for DM-nucleon scattering except with an additional DM scattering form factor. This motivates the definition above of σ¯e\bar{\sigma}_{e}, as when FDM2​(q)=1F_{\rm DM}^{2}(q)=1 we have σ=σ¯e\sigma=\bar{\sigma}_{e}.

V.1.2  Atomic ionization cross section

Turning now to bound electrons with a more complicated wavefunction, the scattering form factors are no longer so simple to evaluate. We will start by assuming free unbound wavefunctions for the outgoing states. It is then convenient to consider a spherical harmonic basis for the final states. Let’s take a brief aside to rewrite the sum over plane wave final states appearing in the cross section:

∫d3​𝐤′(2​π)3e−i𝐤′⋅𝐫ei​𝐤′⋅𝐫′\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{3}{\bf k}^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}e^{-i{{\bf k}^{\prime}}\cdot{\bf r}}e^{i{{\bf k}^{\prime}}\cdot{\bf r}^{\prime}} (130)

as a sum instead over final states labelled by wavenumber k′k^{\prime}, and angular momentum numbers ℓ′,m′\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}. A plane wave can be expanded in terms of spherical wavefunctions

ei​𝐤⋅𝐫=4​π​∑ℓiℓ​jℓ​(k​r)​∑m=−ℓℓYℓ​m∗​(θ𝐤,ϕ𝐤)​Yℓ​m​(θ𝐫,ϕ𝐫)\displaystyle e^{i{{\bf k}}\cdot{\bf r}}=4\pi\sum_{\ell}i^{\ell}j_{\ell}(kr)\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}Y_{\ell m}^{*}(\theta_{{\bf k}},\phi_{{\bf k}})Y_{\ell m}(\theta_{{\bf r}},\phi_{{\bf r}}) (131)

where we used the normalization that ∫d​Ω​|Yℓ​m​(θ,ϕ)|2=1\int d\Omega\,|Y_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi)|^{2}=1 and ∫d​r​r2​jℓ​(k​r)​jℓ​(k′​r)=π/(2​k2)​δ​(k−k′)\int dr\,r^{2}j_{\ell}(kr)j_{\ell}(k^{\prime}r)=\pi/(2k^{2})\delta(k-k^{\prime}). Using these results, we can rewrite Eq. 130 as

∑ℓ′,m′∫d​k′(2​π)3​(k′)2​(4​π​jℓ′​(k′​r)​Yℓ′​m′∗​(θ𝐫,ϕ𝐫))×(4​π​jℓ′​(k′​r′)​Yℓ′​m′​(θ𝐫′,ϕ𝐫′))\displaystyle\sum_{\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}}\int\frac{dk^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}(k^{\prime})^{2}\left(4\pi j_{\ell^{\prime}}(k^{\prime}r)Y^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\theta_{{\bf r}},\phi_{{\bf r}})\right)\times\left(4\pi j_{\ell^{\prime}}(k^{\prime}r^{\prime})Y_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\theta_{{\bf r}^{\prime}},\phi_{{\bf r}^{\prime}})\right) (132)

In this basis, the cross section to excite state jj can be written as

(σ​v)j=∫d3​𝐩′(2​π)3​(k′)2​d​k′(2​π)3​(2​π)​δ​(Δ​Ee−Δ​Eχ)​|ℳfree|216​mχ2​me2​∑ℓ′,m′|fj→k′,ℓ′,m′​(𝐪)|2\displaystyle(\sigma v)_{j}=\int\frac{d^{3}{\bf p}^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{(k^{\prime})^{2}\,dk^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,(2\pi)\delta(\Delta E_{e}-\Delta E_{\chi})\,\frac{|{\cal M}_{\rm free}|^{2}}{16m_{\chi}^{2}m_{e}^{2}}\,\sum_{\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}}|f_{j\to k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}}({\bf q})|^{2} (133)

where the form factor is

|fj→k′,ℓ′,m′​(𝐪)|2\displaystyle|f_{j\to k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}}({\bf q})|^{2} =|∫d3​𝐫​ψj​(𝐫)​Ψk′,ℓ′,m′∗​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫|2\displaystyle=\left|\int d^{3}{\bf r}\,\psi_{j}({\bf r})\,\Psi_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}}^{*}\,e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}}\right|^{2} (134)
=|∫d3​𝐫​ψj​(𝐫)​ 4​π​jℓ′​(k′​r)​Yℓ′​m′∗​(θ𝐫,ϕ𝐫)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫|2.\displaystyle=\left|\int d^{3}{\bf r}\,\psi_{j}({\bf r})\,4\pi j_{\ell^{\prime}}(k^{\prime}r)Y^{*}_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\theta_{{\bf r}},\phi_{{\bf r}})\,e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}}\right|^{2}. (135)

The final state electron energy ER=(k′)2/2​meE_{R}=(k^{\prime})^{2}/2m_{e}, so that we can turn the above into a differential cross section and sum over all bound initial states jj:

d​(σ​v)jd​ln⁡ER=σ¯e16​π​μχ​e2​∫d3​𝐪​δ​(Δ​Ee−Δ​Eχ)​FDM2​(q)​∑ℓ′,m′2​(k′)3(2​π)3​|fj→k′,ℓ′,m′​(𝐪)|2⏟|fjion​(k′,q)|2.\displaystyle\frac{d(\sigma v)_{j}}{d\ln E_{R}}=\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{e}}{16\pi\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int d^{3}{\bf q}\,\delta(\Delta E_{e}-\Delta E_{\chi})\,F_{\rm DM}^{2}(q)\,\underbrace{\sum_{\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}}\frac{2(k^{\prime})^{3}}{(2\pi)^{3}}|f_{j\to k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}}({\bf q})|^{2}}_{\text{\small$|f^{\rm ion}_{j}(k^{\prime},q)|^{2}$}}. (136)

where again we used d3​𝐩′=d3​𝐪d^{3}{\bf p}^{\prime}=d^{3}{\bf q}. Comparing to Eq. 128, we find an extra phase space integral (since the initial state is not a momentum eigenstate) as well as the presence of an atomic ionization form factor |fjion​(k′,q)|2|f^{\rm ion}_{j}(k^{\prime},q)|^{2} for the initial state jj.

As an explicit example, consider scattering from the ground state of Hydrogen into an outgoing ℓ=0,m=0\ell=0,m=0 state with momentum k′k^{\prime}. The exercise is left to the reader to compute this. The result is

|fion​(k′,q)|2=64​(k′​re)3π​[re4​(k′2−q2)2+2​re2​(k′2+q2)+1]2\displaystyle|f^{\rm ion}(k^{\prime},q)|^{2}=\frac{64(k^{\prime}r_{e})^{3}}{\pi\left[r_{e}^{4}(k^{\prime 2}-q^{2})^{2}+2r_{e}^{2}(k^{\prime 2}+q^{2})+1\right]^{2}} (137)

where re=1/(α​me)≈1/3.7r_{e}=1/(\alpha m_{e})\approx 1/3.7 keV is the Bohr radius. This form factor is peaked at q∼k′∼1/req\sim k^{\prime}\sim 1/r_{e}: the outgoing electron wavefunction is correlated with the momentum transfer, while the size of both quantities is set by the initial electron momentum ∼α​me\sim\alpha m_{e}. The total form factor including other ℓ\ell states is shown in Fig. 20 for k′=qk^{\prime}=q, displaying a similar behavior.99 9 Note that we still assume free outgoing states here. The presence of the ion distorts the wavefunction of the outgoing state, such that the basis in Eq. 131 needs to be modified. For further details on this, see Refs. [199, 201]. The typical outgoing electron energy is then k′2/(2​me)∼10k^{\prime 2}/(2m_{e})\sim 10 eV (note that the total deposited energy is the sum of the binding energy plus the outgoing kinetic energy).

This makes explicit the arguments made at the beginning of this section, where we used free electron kinematics and found that the typical energy deposited is around a few eV. This also motivates the definition of the scattering cross section σ¯e\bar{\sigma}_{e} in Eq. 74, since a typical scale for |𝐪|∼α​me|{\bf q}|\sim\alpha m_{e}. To determine the rate in an experiment, there are a few more points to consider. We must also integrate over the DM velocity distribution, discussed already for nuclear recoils in Sec. IV.3.1. However, we can obtain a very rough estimate of the rate below. As estimated around the end of Lecture 3, there are thermal relic (and freeze-in) candidates with sizable DM-electron cross sections, σ¯e≃10−37​cm2\bar{\sigma}_{e}\simeq 10^{-37}{\rm cm}^{2}. Then assuming mχ=10​MeVm_{\chi}=10\,\textrm{MeV} and taking a number of atoms per kg of NT≃1025N_{T}\simeq 10^{25}/kg, we have

R∼NT​ρχmχ​σ¯e​v0≃50−100​events/kg/day.\displaystyle R\sim N_{T}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\bar{\sigma}_{e}\,v_{0}\simeq 50-100\ \textrm{events/kg/day}\,. (138)

Thus, an exposure of around a kg-day is sufficient to observe a DM signal! This can be compared to exposures of 105−10610^{5}-10^{6} kg-day for experiments targeting heavy DM. However, there are new difficulties in detecting low mass DM, namely the issue of lower energy thresholds and control of backgrounds at such low energies.

The calculation performed here can be applied to more realistic targets such as liquid Xenon with a similar minimum ionization energy of ≈12​eV\approx 12\,\textrm{eV} (there are differences in ionization from liquid Xenon compared to a free Xenon atom, but so far this effect has been assumed to be small). Experimental sensitivity to events with a single or a few ionization electrons has been demonstrated with XENON10, XENON100 [201] and more recently DarkSide [202], thus allowing for a novel way to probe light DM scattering off of electrons with an existing experimental setup [203]. Some of these constraints are shown in Fig. 21 for both scattering through a heavy vector mediator and a light vector mediator. The maximum energy deposited per scattering is set by the DM kinetic energy in the halo, which means that for an O⁡(10)O(10) eV ionization threshold we require DM of mass mχ≳few​MeVm_{\chi}\gtrsim{\rm few}\,\textrm{MeV} (see Fig. 19). This is why the XENON10/100 constraints extend at best down to mχ≈m_{\chi}\approx 5 MeV. We note also that the XENON10/100 constraints were limited by the large low-energy backgrounds, and that these experiments were not designed to search for DM-electron scattering. A focused effort in this direction could potentially do much better.

V.1.3  Scattering in a lattice, experimental status, and the sub-MeV frontier

Detecting lighter DM requires systems with smaller thresholds for detectable electron excitations. Note that we should really think of these as quasiparticle excitations, where the quasiparticle is a nearly free state that behaves much like the electron (but could have a smaller effective mass, for instance). We highlight here some of the proposals and considerations.

First of all, reducing the threshold to ∼\sim eV is possible by using semiconductor targets such as Ge and Si, and allow sensitivity to DM masses as low as ∼\sim MeV. Semiconductors have typical electron band gaps of around an eV, and the development of first-principles techniques in calculating band structures has made DM-electron scattering a tractable (if computationally intensive) problem. The detailed theoretical treatment of DM-electron scattering in a crystal can be found in Ref. [200]. Compared to Eq. 133, the difference is that we need a crystal form factor summing over initial and final electron states in the lattice. The electron wavefunctions can be obtained the first-principles techniques mentioned above. Relatedly, we also cannot assume that the outgoing electron energy is a simple function of the momentum.

The SuperCDMS [204] and SENSEI [206, 207] collaborations have recently demonstrated experimental sensitivity to single electron excitations in a silicon target. Fig. 21 shows constraints from surface runs of the two experiments, with only a small exposure. With dedicated underground runs and larger exposure, it is possible to test interesting thermal histories in the near future (see right panel of the figure for some projections). For theoretical studies of the sensitivity of semiconductors to different DM models, see also Refs. [200, 208].

Going to lower thresholds requires considering materials with smaller band gaps for electron excitations. There are proposals to use superconductors [209, 210, 211] and Dirac materials [212], both of which have a gap of around ∼\sim meV and have long lived quasiparticle excitations. If experimental sensitivity to such low energy excitations can be achieved, this would allow detection of DM as light as ∼\sim keV. Similar to the case of semiconductors, DM-electron scattering is heavily reliant on the in-medium electron band structure. The intersection of many-body physics with DM physics is a growing area of research, and applying developments in condensed matter or materials science could lead to further improvements in sensitivity to DM mass/models, reduction in backgrounds, or other advantages.

There is one more important consideration for proposals targeting sub-MeV DM scattering through a kinetically-mixed vector mediator. So far we have accounted for the material/many-body effects only in the wavefunctions of initial and final states, while keeping the matrix element |ℳfree|2|{\cal M}_{\rm free}|^{2}. However, as discussed in Section III.3.1 and detailed in Appendix B, the in-medium electromagnetic polarization tensor can have a significant impact on DM and mediator interactions. For instance, in a metal or a superconductor, electromagnetic interactions are screened by the Thomas-Fermi screening length λTF\lambda_{\rm TF}, where 1/λTF≃1/\lambda_{\rm TF}\simeq few keV for a typical materials. These effects are thus most important for DM below an MeV, where the possible momentum transfers are keV and below. The screening leads to a rough suppression in DM-electron scattering rates by ∼(|𝐪|​λTF)4∼(mχ​v0​λTF)4\sim(|{\bf q}|\,\lambda_{\rm TF})^{4}\sim(m_{\chi}v_{0}\,\lambda_{\rm TF})^{4}. The screening is significantly reduced in Dirac materials [212], which have a linear dispersion for electrons near the Fermi surface. Another way to obtain sensitivity to vector-mediated scattering is to use a polar materials [213, 214]; since these are semiconductors or insulators, the screening is also fairly mild compared to metals. In polar materials, the DM scattering does not create electron excitations (which have a large gap) but instead creates phonon excitations of energies 1−1001-100 meV. We turn to phonon excitations next.

V.2  Phonon couplings

Phonons are collective excitations of the atoms in a solid or liquid, with the simplest examples being sound waves in a medium. There are a number of motivations for considering DM couplings to phonons:

  • •

    Phonons are the relevant degrees of freedom for sufficiently low momentum transfer (typically ≲\lesssim keV, depending on the material), so we are forced to consider DM-phonon interactions for sub-MeV DM.

  • •

    The excitation energy of phonons is small: for sound waves there is no energy gap, while there are also gapped phonon modes with typical energies of 10–100 meV. This is well-suited again for low mass DM, since more of the DM kinetic energy can be deposited (Fig. 19).

  • •

    Since the phonons are excitations of the atoms, a DM-nucleon interaction can create a phonon excitation, allowing an alternate way to probe DM models that does not rely on a DM-electron coupling.

  • •

    A number of DM experiments exploit phonon collection as one of the channels for energy depositions from DM [215, 216, 217], with increasing sensitivity to low energy events in recent years. (Since phonons are also thermally produced, these experiments must be operated in cryogenic environments with T<T< Kelvin.)

In this section, we will focus on phonons in a solid state material – the collective displacements of the atoms in a crystal lattice. We will work through a derivation of the simplest DM-phonon coupling in order to illustrate the basic idea of phonons excitations from DM scattering, and then summarize some of the results in the literature. Before diving in, we clarify one point: what does it really mean when we talk about displacements in a crystal? For a given atom, we can think of the nucleus plus the most tightly bound electrons as being relatively unaffected by the presence of the other atoms. Meanwhile, the outer shell electrons of the atom interact with electrons of neighboring atoms, giving rise to the delocalized electron wavefunctions and complex electron band structure in a material. Therefore, although we usually refer to displacements as atomic displacements, we are really thinking of these as ionic displacements of the nucleus and inner shell electrons.

V.2.1  Acoustic phonons

Introductions to phonon modes can be found in standard references [218], and for completeness we provide a brief review. The system we will consider is a 1D regular lattice of NN atoms of mass MM, shown in the top left of Fig. 22. All of the atoms are identical, so the unit cell has a size aa (the lattice spacing) and contains one atom. Each atom ii has a possible displacement from its equilibrium position, denoted by uiu_{i}. The Hamiltonian for this system is modeled with an effective potential for the relative displacements of neighboring atoms:

H=∑i12​M​u˙i2+12​keff​(ui+1−ui)2+…\displaystyle H=\sum_{i}\frac{1}{2}M\dot{u}_{i}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}k_{\rm eff}(u_{i+1}-u_{i})^{2}+... (139)

where the ... are possible higher order terms in the displacements. Those terms could lead to three-phonon couplings, for instance.

We will take the continuum limit for this system, or equivalently consider long-wavelength excitations, so that the displacement field u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) is a function of position and time. Writing Δ​x=a\Delta x=a, the sum over positions ii can be replaced by an integral over xx:

H=∫d​x​(12​ρ​u˙2+12​k~eff​(∇u)2)\displaystyle H=\int dx\ \left(\frac{1}{2}\rho\dot{u}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\tilde{k}_{\rm eff}(\nabla u)^{2}\right) (140)

where ρ=M/a\rho=M/a is the mass per unit length, k~eff=a​keff\tilde{k}_{\rm eff}=ak_{\rm eff}, and we have replaced the finite difference with a gradient. Equivalently, introducing a minus sign for the potential, the Lagrangian for the system is:

ℒ=∫d​x​(12​ρ​u˙2−12​k~eff​(∇u)2).\displaystyle{\cal L}=\int dx\ \left(\frac{1}{2}\rho\dot{u}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\tilde{k}_{\rm eff}(\nabla u)^{2}\right). (141)

This describes a free, massless particle with linear dispersion, ωq=cs​|𝐪|=cs​q\omega_{q}=c_{s}|{\bf q}|=c_{s}q, and speed of sound cs=k~eff/ρ=a2​keff/Mc_{s}=\sqrt{\tilde{k}_{\rm eff}/\rho}=\sqrt{a^{2}k_{\rm eff}/M}. The mode is otherwise known as an acoustic phonon, with an energy that goes to zero in the q→0q\to 0 limit. This reflects the fact that the acoustic phonon is a Goldstone boson associated with spontaneous breaking of translational symmetry. As q→0q\to 0, all atoms are displaced by the same amount and the arrangement is physically equivalent to the original ground state.

The quantized displacement field (phonon) is written in a standard way, in terms of a mode expansion in the interaction picture:

u⁡(x,t)=∑j12​N​a​ρ​ωqj​(a^qj​ei​qj​x−i​ωqj​t+h.c.)\displaystyle u(x,t)=\sum_{j}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2Na\rho\omega_{q_{j}}}}\left(\hat{a}_{q_{j}}\ e^{i{q_{j}}x-i\omega_{q_{j}}t}+\textrm{h.c.}\right) (142)
=a​Nρ​∫d​q(2​π)​12​ωq​(a^q​ei​q​x−i​ωq​t+h.c.)\displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{aN}}{\sqrt{\rho}}\int\frac{dq}{(2\pi)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\omega_{q}}}\left(\hat{a}_{q}\ e^{iqx-i\omega_{q}t}+\textrm{h.c.}\right) (143)

with creation and annihilation operators a^q,a^q†\hat{a}_{q},\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{q} satisfying the commutation relations [a^q,a^q′†]=δq,q′[\hat{a}_{q},\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{q^{\prime}}]=\delta_{q,q^{\prime}}. In the first line, we have written the expansion in terms of a discrete sum – this reflects the actual discrete lattice, with qj=2​π​j/(a​N)q_{j}=2\pi j/(aN) for a lattice of length a​NaN. In the second line, we have given the continuum limit result. (If the factor of a​N\sqrt{aN} looks funny in the continuum limit, it is because in the QFT convention we typically normalize the creation and annihilation operators differently, [a^q,a^q′†]=2​π​δ​(q−q′)→V=a​N[\hat{a}_{q},\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{q^{\prime}}]=2\pi\delta(q-q^{\prime})\to V=aN when q=q′q=q^{\prime}, see Appendix A. This would remove the factor.) As an exercise, you can check that plugging the above expansion into the Hamiltonian gives, in the discrete limit:

H=∑jωqj​(a^qj†​a^qj+12).\displaystyle H=\sum_{j}\omega_{q_{j}}\left(\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{q_{j}}\hat{a}_{q_{j}}+\frac{1}{2}\right). (144)

We have found that the excitations are described by phonons created by the a^q†\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{q} operator.

The energy eigenvalues ωqj\omega_{q_{j}} can be solved for exactly, see Ref. [218]. The right panel of Fig. 22 shows the exact phonon band structure over the first Brillouin zone (BZ), accounting for the lattice periodicity. In the long-wavelength limit q≪π/aq\ll\pi/a, we see the linear dispersion expected for Goldstone modes. The size of the first BZ is set by π/a\pi/a; for a typical material a∼fewa\sim{\rm few} Å, and so q≲q\lesssim keV in the first BZ.

Going to three spatial dimensions, the displacement field becomes a vector field 𝐮⁡(𝐱,t){\bf u}({\bf x},t) and there are more phonon branches corresponding to the additional degrees of freedom. The band structure for a possible direct detection material (GaAs) is shown in the right panel of Fig. 23, with the phonon energies plotted against a specific path within the first BZ. Here the q→0q\to 0 limit is labelled by the Γ\Gamma point, and there are three acoustic modes for a 3-dimensional lattice – two transverse acoustic (TA) branches where the oscillation of the atoms is perpendicular to 𝐪{\bf q} and one longitudinal acoustic (LA) branch. The acoustic modes have linear dispersions for sufficiently small qq, although the sound speed is different for transverse vs. longitudinal phonons. Because the unit cell for GaAs contains more than one atom, it is seen that there are also optical phonon branches (LO and TO), which we discuss further below. Before introducing this feature, we turn to the coupling of a DM candidate with acoustic phonons.

V.2.2  Dark matter coupling to acoustic phonons

To describe the interaction of a DM candidate with a phonon, we must first determine the underlying DM interactions with electrons and nuclei. To start, a simple case is fermion DM with a scalar mediator coupling to nucleons:

ℒ⊃−mχ​χ¯​χ−12​mϕ2​ϕ2−yn​(n¯​n+p¯​p)​ϕ−yχ​ϕ​χ¯​χ\displaystyle{\cal L}\supset-m_{\chi}\bar{\chi}\chi-\frac{1}{2}m_{\phi}^{2}\phi^{2}-y_{n}(\bar{n}n+\bar{p}p)\phi-y_{\chi}\phi\bar{\chi}\chi (145)

for both protons and neutrons. For this model, DM scattering into acoustic phonons has been studied in polar materials [213, 214] and superfluid helium [219, 220, 221]. Of course, superfluid helium is not a crystal, but acoustic phonons are also present and a number of techniques are similar.

Since we are working in the non-relativistic limit, we can use the interaction Hamiltonian to compute the scattering rate. This will also make it straightforward to write the operators in terms of phonon creation and annihilation operators a^𝐪†,a^𝐪\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\bf q},\hat{a}_{\bf q} for 3D momentum vector 𝐪{\bf q}. For a massive mediator ϕ\phi, the Hamiltonian for the DM-nucleon interaction can be written in the non-relativistic limit as

yχ​ynmϕ2​∫d3​𝐫​χ¯​χ​(n¯​n+p¯​p).\displaystyle\frac{y_{\chi}y_{n}}{m_{\phi}^{2}}\int d^{3}{\bf r}\ \bar{\chi}\chi(\bar{n}n+\bar{p}p). (146)

The operator n¯​n+p¯​p\bar{n}n+\bar{p}p becomes the number density of nucleons in the non-relativistic limit. Since we are dealing with low momentum transfer qq, we can sum coherently over all of the nucleons in a given nucleus NN with mass number AA. The interaction can then be written in terms the number density operator ρ⁡(𝐫)\rho({\bf r}) for the nuclei:

ℋI=A​yχ​ynmϕ2​∫d3​𝐫​χ¯​χ​N¯​N→A​yχ​ynmϕ2​∫d3​𝐫​χ¯​χ​ρ​(𝐫),\displaystyle{\cal H}_{I}=\frac{Ay_{\chi}y_{n}}{m_{\phi}^{2}}\int d^{3}{\bf r}\ \bar{\chi}\chi\,\bar{N}N\to\frac{Ay_{\chi}y_{n}}{m_{\phi}^{2}}\int d^{3}{\bf r}\ \bar{\chi}\chi\,\rho({\bf r}), (147)

with additional terms if multiple types of nuclei are present. We consider just one type of atom here.

In order to make a connection with the QM language used in the condensed matter literature, we perform a mode expansion for the fermionic χ\chi field into creation and annihilation operators b^𝐩,s†,b^𝐩,s\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{{\bf p},s},\hat{b}_{{\bf p},s} for the DM, as well as analogous operators c^𝐩,s†,c^𝐩,s\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{{\bf p},s},\hat{c}_{{\bf p},s} for antiparticles. Explicitly, we use the expansion in the interaction picture:

χ⁡(𝐫,t)=V​∫d3​𝐩(2​π)3​12​ω𝐩​∑s(b^𝐩,s​us​(p)​e−i​ω𝐩​t+i​𝐩⋅𝐫+c^𝐩,s†​vs​(p)​ei​ω𝐩​t−i​𝐩⋅𝐫)\displaystyle\chi({\bf r},t)=\sqrt{V}\int\frac{d^{3}{\bf p}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\bf p}}}\sum_{s}\left(\hat{b}_{{\bf p},s}\,u^{s}(p)\,e^{-i\omega_{\bf p}t+i{\bf p}\cdot{\bf r}}\,+\,\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{{\bf p},s}\,v^{s}(p)\,e^{i\omega_{\bf p}t-i{\bf p}\cdot{\bf r}}\right) (148)

and similar for χ¯​(𝐫,t)\bar{\chi}({\bf r},t). The factor of V\sqrt{V} is because we are using the non-relativistic normalization for the operators where {b^𝐩,s,b^𝐩′,s′†}=δ𝐩,𝐩′​δs,s′\{\hat{b}_{{\bf p},s},\hat{b}_{{\bf p^{\prime}},s^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\}=\delta_{\bf p,{\bf p}^{\prime}}\delta_{s,s^{\prime}}. For convenience, we consider only the scattering of DM particles in the discussion below; similar interaction terms are present for DM antiparticles.

The next step is to take the nonrelativistic limit and rewrite the interaction Hamiltonian in terms of a discrete sum for the finite volume VV. The convention to go between continuum limit and discrete sum is given in Appendix A for convenience. This is roughly the reverse of the procedure in the acoustic phonon toy model above. (Our approach of starting from the relativistic Lorentz invariant theory may seem backwards, but we are assuming the typical reader is coming from a particle physics background.) Inserting Eq. 148 into Eq. 147 then gives

ℋI=A​yχ​ynmϕ2​1V​∑s∑𝐩,𝐩′b^𝐩′,s†​b^𝐩,s​∫d3​𝐫​e[i⁡(𝐩−𝐩′)⋅𝐫−i⁡(ω𝐩−ω𝐩′)​t]​ρ​(𝐫).\displaystyle{\cal H}_{I}=\frac{Ay_{\chi}y_{n}}{m_{\phi}^{2}}\frac{1}{V}\sum_{s}\sum_{\bf p,\bf p^{\prime}}\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{{\bf p^{\prime}},s}\,\hat{b}_{{\bf p},s}\,\int d^{3}{\bf r}\,e^{\left[i({\bf p}-{\bf p}^{\prime})\cdot{\bf r}-i(\omega_{\bf p}-\omega_{{\bf p}^{\prime}})t\right]}\,\rho({\bf r}). (149)

The integral is proportional to a Fourier transform of the density field. Thus a DM scattering creates a density excitation with momentum 𝐩−𝐩′=𝐪{{\bf p}-{\bf p}^{\prime}}={\bf q}. In the limit of a dilute gas of atoms, then the density excitation would be just a single atom that has been given a momentum kick. However, in treating a lattice or a liquid, we must translate the density excitation into the creation of a phonon.

Since the size of a typical nucleus is a few fm, much smaller than the interparticle spacing, we can approximate the density field as a sum over delta functions:

ρ⁡(𝐫)=∑Jδ⁡(𝐫−𝐫J),𝐫J≡𝐫J0+𝐮J\displaystyle\rho({\bf r})=\sum_{J}\delta\left({\bf r}-{\bf r}_{J}\right),\ \ {\bf r}_{J}\equiv{\bf r}_{J}^{0}+{\bf u}_{J} (150)

where we have decomposed 𝐫J{\bf r}_{J}, the position of ion JJ, into its equilibrium position 𝐫J0{\bf r}_{J}^{0} and displacement 𝐮J​(t){\bf u}_{J}(t). Inserting this density field into Eq. 149, we can now write the Hamiltonian in terms of 𝐮J{{\bf u}_{J}} and brazenly take the limit of small 𝐮J{{\bf u}}_{J}:

ℋI\displaystyle{\cal H}_{I} =A​yχ​ynmϕ2​1V​∑s∑𝐩,𝐩′b^𝐩′,s†​b^𝐩,s​e−i⁡(ω𝐩−ω𝐩′)​t​∑Jexp⁡[i⁡(𝐩−𝐩′)⋅(𝐫J0+𝐮J)]\displaystyle=\frac{Ay_{\chi}y_{n}}{m_{\phi}^{2}}\frac{1}{V}\sum_{s}\sum_{\bf p,\bf p^{\prime}}\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{{\bf p^{\prime}},s}\,\hat{b}_{{\bf p},s}\,e^{-i(\omega_{\bf p}-\omega_{{\bf p}^{\prime}})t}\,\sum_{J}\exp\left[i({\bf p}-{\bf p}^{\prime})\cdot({\bf r}_{J}^{0}+{\bf u}_{J})\right] (151)
→A​yχ​ynmϕ2​1V​∑s∑𝐩,𝐩′b^𝐩′,s†​b^𝐩,s​e−i⁡(ω𝐩−ω𝐩′)​t​∑Jei⁡(𝐩−𝐩′)⋅𝐫J0​(𝐩−𝐩′)⋅𝐮J​(t).\displaystyle\to\frac{Ay_{\chi}y_{n}}{m_{\phi}^{2}}\frac{1}{V}\sum_{s}\sum_{\bf p,\bf p^{\prime}}\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{{\bf p^{\prime}},s}\,\hat{b}_{{\bf p},s}\,e^{-i(\omega_{\bf p}-\omega_{{\bf p}^{\prime}})t}\,\sum_{J}e^{i({\bf p}-{\bf p}^{\prime})\cdot{\bf r}_{J}^{0}}\,({\bf p}-{\bf p}^{\prime})\cdot{\bf u}_{J}(t)\ . (152)

In addition, we have dropped the piece independent of 𝐮J{\bf u}_{J}, since this doesn’t lead to any scattering.

For the next step, we will gloss over some of the details and instead refer the interested reader to Ref. [214]. (A warning that the notation is not always identical, in order to simplify the presentation here.) The basic idea is the following: similar to the mode decomposition given in Eq. 143, the displacement 𝐮J{{\bf u}_{J}} can be expanded as a sum over creation and annihilation operators for phonons of momentum 𝐪{{\bf q}}. In a 3D lattice with NN atoms, and including a phonon eigenvector 𝐞𝐪,ν{\bf e}_{{\bf q},\nu} to account for the phonon polarization,

𝐮J​(t)=∑𝐪,ν12​N​M​ω𝐪,ν​(a^𝐪​𝐞𝐪,ν​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫J0−i​ω𝐪,ν​t+h.c.).\displaystyle{\bf u}_{J}(t)=\sum_{{\bf q},\nu}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2NM\omega_{{\bf q},\nu}}}\left(\hat{a}_{{\bf q}}\,{\bf e}_{{\bf q},\nu}\ e^{i{{\bf q}}\cdot{{\bf r}}^{0}_{J}-i\omega_{{\bf q},\nu}t}+\textrm{h.c.}\right). (153)

Here ν\nu is an index labeling the different phonon mode branches and ω𝐪,ν\omega_{{\bf q},\nu} is the energy of the phonon in branch ν\nu with momentum 𝐪{\bf q}.

Inserting the mode expansion of 𝐮J{{\bf u}_{J}} into Eq. 152 and performing the sum over all J=1​…​NJ=1...N enforces the momentum conservation condition. We see that the interaction Hamiltonian includes a term where a phonon of momentum 𝐪{{\bf q}} is excited by the DM:

ℋI=A​yχ​ynmϕ2​NV​∑s∑𝐩,𝐪,νb^𝐩−𝐪,s†​b^𝐩,s​a^𝐪†​𝐪⋅𝐞𝐪,ν∗2​M​ω𝐪,ν​e−i⁡(ω𝐩−ω𝐩−𝐪−ω𝐪,ν)​t\displaystyle{\cal H}_{I}=\frac{Ay_{\chi}y_{n}}{m_{\phi}^{2}}\frac{\sqrt{N}}{V}\sum_{s}\sum_{\bf p,\bf q,\nu}\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{{\bf p}-{\bf q},s}\,\hat{b}_{{\bf p},s}\,\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\bf q}\ \frac{{\bf q}\cdot{\bf e}^{*}_{{\bf q},\nu}}{\sqrt{2M\omega_{\bf q,\nu}}}\ e^{-i(\omega_{\bf p}-\omega_{{\bf p}-{\bf q}}-\omega_{{\bf q},\nu})t} (154)

where 𝐪=𝐩−𝐩′{\bf q}={\bf p}-{\bf p}^{\prime} and 𝐞𝐪{\bf e}_{\bf q} is a normalized eigenvector for the phonon with momentum 𝐪{\bf q}. At this point, you may be concerned about the factors of N/V\sqrt{N}/V where we will take the V,N→∞V,N\to\infty limit. This will drop out in the end; in computing the DM scattering, we will sum the matrix element squared over all excited phonon states, where the density of states scales as NN in the infinite volume limit.

For a given DM particle with momentum 𝐩=mχ​𝐯{\bf p}=m_{\chi}{\bf v}, the above interaction Hamiltonian gives rise to a (spin-averaged) transition rate of

Γ⁡(𝐯)\displaystyle\Gamma({\bf v}) =2​π​A2​yχ2​yn2mϕ4​NV2​∑𝐪,ν|𝐪⋅𝐞𝐪,ν∗|22​M​ω𝐪,ν​δ​(ω𝐩−ω𝐩−𝐪−ω𝐪,ν),\displaystyle=2\pi\,\frac{A^{2}y_{\chi}^{2}y_{n}^{2}}{m_{\phi}^{4}}\frac{N}{V^{2}}\sum_{{\bf q},\nu}\frac{|{\bf q}\cdot{\bf e}^{*}_{{\bf q},\nu}|^{2}}{2M\omega_{{\bf q},\nu}}\,\delta(\omega_{\bf p}-\omega_{{\bf p}-{\bf q}}-\omega_{{\bf q},\nu}),
=2​π​A2​yχ2​yn2mϕ4​1Ω​∑ν∫d3​𝐪(2​π)3​|𝐪⋅𝐞𝐪,ν∗|22​M​ω𝐪,ν​δ​(ω𝐩−ω𝐩−𝐪−ω𝐪,ν)\displaystyle=2\pi\,\frac{A^{2}y_{\chi}^{2}y_{n}^{2}}{m_{\phi}^{4}}\frac{1}{\Omega}\sum_{\nu}\int\frac{d^{3}{\bf q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{|{\bf q}\cdot{\bf e}^{*}_{{\bf q},\nu}|^{2}}{2M\omega_{{\bf q},\nu}}\,\delta(\omega_{\bf p}-\omega_{{\bf p}-{\bf q}}-\omega_{{\bf q},\nu}) (155)

(i.e., Fermi’s Golden Rule for a time-dependent interaction). Note that in the second line, we took the continuum limit and defined the unit cell volume Ω≡V/N∼a3\Omega\equiv V/N\sim a^{3} for lattice spacing aa.

The above result captures the qualitative form of the scattering rate, but is only approximate. Aside from the simplification in Eq. 152, we did not distinguish between different atoms inside a primitive cell of a crystal lattice. The full derivation and expansion in small 𝐮J​(t){\bf u}_{J}(t) is more lengthy. It accounts for the fact that there is also a typical ‘zero-point’ motion of the ions in the lattice, which is encapsulated in the Debye Waller factors Wα​(𝐪)W_{\alpha}({\bf q}). More generally, scattering off nuclei is typically described in terms of the dynamic structure factor S⁡(𝐪,ω)S({\bf q},\omega). For scattering into an acoustic phonon, this quantity can be written in the long-wavelength limit as

S⁡(𝐪,ω)≈12​ω𝐪,ν​|∑αAαMα​𝐪⋅𝐞𝐪,να​e−Wα​(𝐪)|2​δ​(ω𝐪,ν−ω)\displaystyle S({\bf q},\omega)\approx\frac{1}{2\omega_{{\bf q},\nu}}\left|\sum_{\alpha}\frac{A_{\alpha}}{\sqrt{M_{\alpha}}}{\bf q}\cdot{\bf e}^{\alpha}_{{\bf q},\nu}\,e^{-W_{\alpha}({\bf q})}\right|^{2}\delta(\omega_{{\bf q},\nu}-\omega) (156)

where α\alpha runs over all atoms within a primitive unit cell. The complete results and derivation can be found in Ref. [214], which was based on the review by Schober [222].

Summarizing our efforts here, the DM scattering rate for a general lattice is given in terms of the dynamic structure factor:

Γ=2​π​(2​π​bχ)2mχ2​1Ω​∫BZd3​𝐪(2​π)3​S​(𝐪,ω),\displaystyle\Gamma=2\pi\frac{(2\pi b_{\chi})^{2}}{m_{\chi}^{2}}\frac{1}{\Omega}\int_{\rm BZ}\frac{d^{3}{\bf q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,S({\bf q},\omega), (157)

where we have defined a DM scattering length bχb_{\chi}, such that the single nucleon cross section is given by σn=4​π​bχ2=yχ2​yn2​mχ2/(π​mϕ4)\sigma_{n}=4\pi b_{\chi}^{2}=y_{\chi}^{2}y_{n}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}/(\pi m_{\phi}^{4}) for sub-GeV fermion DM scattering through a massive mediator. In the equation above, it is implicit that 𝐪=𝐩−𝐩′{\bf q}={\bf p}-{\bf p}^{\prime} is the momentum transfer and ω=ω𝐩−ω𝐩−𝐪\omega=\omega_{\bf p}-\omega_{{\bf p}-{\bf q}} is the energy deposited.

The total scattering rate per unit target mass is obtained by integrating over the DM velocity distribution,

R\displaystyle R =1ρT​ρχmχ​∫d3​𝐯​f​(𝐯)​Γ​(𝐯)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\rho_{T}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\int d^{3}{\bf v}\,f({\bf v})\,\Gamma({\bf v}) (158)
=ρχmχ​σn4​π​mχ2​∫d3​𝐯​f​(𝐯)​(1ρT​Ω​∫BZd3​𝐪​S​(𝐪,ω))\displaystyle=\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\sigma_{n}}{4\pi m_{\chi}^{2}}\int d^{3}{\bf v}\,f({\bf v})\left(\frac{1}{\rho_{T}\Omega}\int_{\rm BZ}d^{3}{\bf q}\,S({\bf q},\omega)\right) (159)

where ρT\rho_{T} is the target mass density. This is the basis of the approach to DM-phonon scattering in a lattice used in Ref. [214]. Eq. 159 can also be applied to superfluid He, even though there is no lattice. A number of works have used analytic or numerical results for the dynamic structure factor to show that multiphonon creation in superfluid He could be exploited for sub-MeV DM scattering [219, 220, 221].

Let’s make a heuristic estimate of the total rate for scattering into a long wavelength acoustic phonon with energy ω=meV\omega={\rm meV}. The acoustic phonon dispersion is given by ω𝐪=cs​q\omega_{{\bf q}}=c_{s}q with cs∼10−5c_{s}\sim 10^{-5} in a typical material. Assuming each unit cell consists of a single atom of mass MNM_{N}, the integral over the dynamic structure factor can be simplified to

∫BZd3​𝐪​S​(𝐪,ω)≃4​π​∫d​q​q2​q​A22​cs​MN​δ​(cs​q−ω)=4​π​A2MN​ω32​cs5.\displaystyle\int_{\rm BZ}d^{3}{\bf q}\,S({\bf q},\omega)\simeq 4\pi\int dq\,q^{2}\frac{qA^{2}}{2c_{s}M_{N}}\delta(c_{s}q-\omega)=\frac{4\pi A^{2}}{M_{N}}\frac{\omega^{3}}{2c_{s}^{5}}\ . (160)

With this, we can get a rough idea of the rate for MeV DM scattering off a target with A=100A=100 and MN=A​mnM_{N}=Am_{n}:

R⁡(ω=meV)\displaystyle R(\omega={\rm meV}) ≃ρχmχ​σnmχ2​1ρT​Ω​A2MN​ω32​cs5\displaystyle\simeq\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\sigma_{n}}{m_{\chi}^{2}}\frac{1}{\rho_{T}\Omega}\frac{A^{2}}{M_{N}}\frac{\omega^{3}}{2c_{s}^{5}} (161)
=2​eventskg⋅day​(σn10−41​cm2)​(MeVmχ)3​(10−5cs)5​(3​g/cm3×Å3ρT​Ω).\displaystyle=2\,\frac{{\rm events}}{{\rm kg}\cdot{\rm day}}\left(\frac{\sigma_{n}}{10^{-41}{\rm cm}^{2}}\right)\left(\frac{\textrm{MeV}}{m_{\chi}}\right)^{3}\left(\frac{10^{-5}}{c_{s}}\right)^{5}\left(\frac{3\,{\rm g/cm}^{3}\times\textrm{\AA}^{3}}{\rho_{T}\Omega}\right). (162)

We have neglected the DM velocity integral for this estimate. Remarkably, we find that a cross section of σn≃10−41​cm2\sigma_{n}\simeq 10^{-41}{\rm cm}^{2} could be probed with a kg-day exposure in a low-threshold experiment. Of course, this assumes zero background and requires detectability of ∼\sim meV phonon excitations, which is an enormous experimental challenge. However, it is promising to see that OO(kg) size targets could be sensitive to relatively small DM scattering cross sections.

  • ⋆\star

    Exercise: Suppose DM couples to nucleons via a light mediator. Taking the massless mediator limit, there is an additional momentum-transfer dependence which can be parameterized by including a DM form factor FDM2​(𝐪)=(mχ​v0)4/|𝐪|4F^{2}_{\rm DM}({\bf q})=(m_{\chi}v_{0})^{4}/|{\bf q}|^{4} with v0=220v_{0}=220 km/s. (See for example the analogous definition for electron scattering in Eq. 126.) Estimate the acoustic phonon excitation rate for σn≃10−41\sigma_{n}\simeq 10^{-41} cm2, where now σn\sigma_{n} is a reference cross section at |𝐪|ref=mχ​v0|{\bf q}|_{\rm ref}=m_{\chi}v_{0}.

From Eq. 162, one might think the sensitivity improves dramatically with smaller mχm_{\chi} and csc_{s}. However, this is not really case once we integrate over the DM velocity distribution. For smaller mχm_{\chi}, the available phase space for creating an excitation of ω=meV\omega={\rm meV} also becomes smaller. In particular, the maximum energy deposition from DM scattering can be estimated as

ωmax=cs​qmax≲2​cs​mχ​v∼few​meV×mχ100​keV×cs10−5\displaystyle\omega_{\rm max}=c_{s}q_{\rm max}\lesssim 2c_{s}m_{\chi}v\sim{\rm few}\,{\rm meV}\times\frac{m_{\chi}}{100\,{\rm keV}}\times\frac{c_{s}}{10^{-5}} (163)

which scales as mχm_{\chi} and csc_{s}. Similarly, for smaller csc_{s} the phonon energies are smaller for a given momentum transfer. This again leads to a phase space suppression since we typically have to impose a minimum recoil energy, which is very optimistically ω≃\omega\simeq meV. One can also expect some correlation of the target nucleus mass with the speed of sound, so it is not obvious that increasing AA leads to a larger rate. The yield-limited sensitivity from more detailed calculations for DM scattering via a light mediator is shown in Fig. 24. This result is for a GaAs target which has cs≈1.3×10−5c_{s}\approx 1.3\times 10^{-5}. For a sapphire (Al2O3) target, which has cs≈3.3×10−5c_{s}\approx 3.3\times 10^{-5}, the reach is quite similar [214].

V.2.3  Optical phonons

A realistic 3D lattice has more than one atom per unit cell, resulting in additional phonon branches associated with the relative motions of the atoms within the cell. We will illustrate this briefly with the toy 1D lattice, shown in Fig. 25. Taking the same effective spring constant everywhere for simplicity, the Hamiltonian for this lattice then has the form

H=∑i12​M1​u˙2​i2+12​M2​w˙2​i+12+12​keff​(u2​i−w2​i+1)2+12​keff​(u2​i+2−w2​i+1)2\displaystyle H=\sum_{i}\frac{1}{2}M_{1}\dot{u}_{2i}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}M_{2}\dot{w}_{2i+1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}k_{\rm eff}(u_{2i}-w_{2i+1})^{2}+\frac{1}{2}k_{\rm eff}(u_{2i+2}-w_{2i+1})^{2}\, (164)

where i=0..N−1i=0..N-1 is an index running over all unit cells. As before, the exact dispersions can be derived in this toy model, see Ref. [218]. In order to put things in a form more familiar to field theorists, we can again turn this into a Lagrangian by taking a continuum limit. Define fields u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) for the displacements of the two atoms in the unit cell. Then the Lagrangian can be written as

∫d​x​(ρ12​u˙​(x,t)2+ρ22​w˙​(x,t)2−keff2​a​[u⁡(x,t)−w⁡(x+a2,t)]2−keff2​a​[u⁡(x,t)−w⁡(x−a2,t)]2)\displaystyle\int dx\left(\tfrac{\rho_{1}}{2}\dot{u}(x,t)^{2}+\tfrac{\rho_{2}}{2}\dot{w}(x,t)^{2}-\tfrac{k_{\rm eff}}{2a}\left[u(x,t)-w(x+\tfrac{a}{2},t)\right]^{2}-\tfrac{k_{\rm eff}}{2a}\left[u(x,t)-w(x-\tfrac{a}{2},t)\right]^{2}\right)

where we have taken care that the displacements of the atoms u2​iu_{2i} and w2​i+1w_{2i+1} are the displacements of the fields at positions xx and x+a/2x+a/2, respectively. The densities are ρ1=M1/a\rho_{1}=M_{1}/a and ρ2=M2/a\rho_{2}=M_{2}/a.

We substitute the following expansion for the ww field in the long wavelength limit:

w(x±a2,t)≈w(x,t)±a2∇w(x,t)+a28∇2w(x,t).\displaystyle w(x\pm\tfrac{a}{2},t)\approx w(x,t)\pm\tfrac{a}{2}\nabla w(x,t)+\tfrac{a^{2}}{8}\nabla^{2}w(x,t). (165)

Then this Lagrangian can be rewritten as

∫dx(12ρ1u˙2+12ρ2w˙2−k~effa2(u−w)2−k~eff4(∇u∇w))\displaystyle\int dx\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho_{1}\dot{u}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\rho_{2}\dot{w}^{2}-\frac{\tilde{k}_{\rm eff}}{a^{2}}(u-w)^{2}-\frac{\tilde{k}_{\rm eff}}{4}(\nabla u\nabla w)\right) (166)

where k~eff=keff​a\tilde{k}_{\rm eff}=k_{\rm eff}a as before. This time we find an apparent mass mixing for the u⁡(x),w⁡(x)u(x),w(x) fields. In the limit ρ1=ρ2\rho_{1}=\rho_{2}, there is one massless mode ∝(u+w)/2\propto(u+w)/\sqrt{2} (the Goldstone mode where all the atoms in a unit cell move in phase) and one massive/gapped mode ∝(u−w)/2\propto(u-w)/\sqrt{2} (where the atoms in a unit cell move out of the phase).

    ωacoustic\displaystyle\omega_{\rm acoustic} ≈|𝐪|​k~eff2​(ρ1+ρ2),u⁡(x)=w⁡(x)\displaystyle\approx|{\bf q}|\sqrt{\frac{\tilde{k}_{\rm eff}}{2(\rho_{1}+\rho_{2})}}\quad,\quad u(x)=w(x) (167)

The exact dispersion relations for the toy model are shown in the right panel Fig. 25. As before, the slope of the acoustic phonon dispersion is typically given by the speed of sound, around 10−5−10−610^{-5}-10^{-6}. The gapped optical phonon mode typically has energies of 10–100 meV in crystals.

Consider the kinematics of DM scattering, it can be even more advantageous to search for excitations into optical phonons. The reason is that the optical phonon has an approximately constant energy as q→0q\to 0. For sub-MeV DM, q≪q\ll keV and so more energy can be deposited by exciting an optical phonon mode compared to an acoustic phonon mode. This is helpful since the experimental threshold does not have to be quite so low.

In addition, for compound materials such as GaAs the different atoms within the unit cell generally have different effective charges. These materials are also known as polar materials. The Born effective charges ZZ describe the induced polarization due to the displacement of an atom. For GaAs, these are equal and opposite with |Z|≈2.27|Z|\approx 2.27. As a result, the out-of-phase oscillations in an optical phonon can be viewed as oscillating dipoles. DM that interacts via a kinetically-mixed dark photon can thus create these dipole excitations, whereas it may not have enough energy to create an electron excitation (the gap for electron excitations in polar materials is usually at least eV). The sensitivity from optical phonon excitations in GaAs is shown in Fig. 24, where it is particularly promising for the vector portal model.

DM-phonon excitations have only been explored for a few materials so far, and it is an interesting question as to how to optimize for a target material sensitive to different types of phonon scattering. The directional dependence of phonon modes in a crystal also means it may be possible to observe a directional signal from DM scattering [214]. Finally, the phonon properties are important in determining the experimental prospects of detecting low energy excitations. See Ref. [213] for a brief discussion of the detector concept and some of the relevant backgrounds.

V.3  The ultralight frontier and conclusions

We have focused on summarizing the basic physics of sub-GeV DM scattering off electrons and phonons. Other quasiparticle excitations may also be promising for different types of DM interactions! In the case of electrons and phonons, the same experimental proposals are also sensitive to much lighter DM through an absorption process. The idea is similar to the photoelectric effect, where bosonic DM is absorbed to create electron and phonon excitations. In many cases the DM absorption rate can thus be related to the optical absorption properties of the material. This idea has been explored in a range of targets [116, 211, 208, 223, 213, 212, 224, 214] for DM down to the ∼\sim meV scale, and experiments have recently set direct detection limits on eV-scale DM [205, 225, 204].

The quest to detect even lower mass DM has also proceeded with great fervor recently. There are methods to search for DM as light as the fuzzy DM limit (∼10−22\sim 10^{-22} eV), as well as those that target the QCD axion as a DM candidate specifically [22, 226, 79]. As with sub-GeV DM scattering, some of these take advantage of technological developments in neighboring fields of physics. The landscape of experimental and observational probes of DM is just as varied as the landscape of models. It is an exciting time in the search for DM, and with some luck and thoughtfulness, we may look forward to some of our efforts bearing fruit.

Appendix A Units and Conventions

In this appendix, we summarize some conventions and other facts that may be useful in reading these notes or exploring some of the topics in more depth. Table 3 gives some unit conversions to help in translating between cosmology, condensed matter, and particle physics.

Sub-GeV direct detection often requires referring to the condensed matter literature, and we note that the units in condensed matter often assume cgs-Gaussian units. However, these notes (and most papers in the direct detection literature) follow the convention in the particle physics community in using Lorentz-Heaviside units:

e\displaystyle e =4​π​α​ℏ​c,Lorentz−Heaviside\displaystyle=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha\hbar c}\ ,\ \ \ {\rm Lorentz-Heaviside}
e\displaystyle e =α​ℏ​c,cgs−Gaussian\displaystyle=\sqrt{\alpha\hbar c}\ ,\ \ \ \ \ \ \ {\rm cgs-Gaussian}

In lecture 5, we switch between discrete sums in finite volume and integrating over continuous variables in the infinite volume limit. For reference, the relations are:

δ𝐤,𝐤′\displaystyle\delta_{{\bf k},{\bf k}^{\prime}} →(2​π)3V​δ(3)​(𝐤−𝐤′)\displaystyle\to\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{V}\delta^{(3)}({\bf k}-{\bf k}^{\prime}) (170)
a^𝐪\displaystyle\hat{a}_{{\bf q}} →a^𝐪V\displaystyle\to\frac{\hat{a}_{{\bf q}}}{\sqrt{V}} (171)

Appendix B In-medium dark photon couplings and photon polarization

A kinetically mixed dark photon is a nearly ubiquitous feature in models of dark sectors. As discussed in Sec. III.3.1, the appropriate couplings in a given scenario depend sensitively on the photon polarization tensor Πμ​ν\Pi^{\mu\nu}. In this appendix, we examine the effective in-medium couplings of the dark photon and also provide a summary of the behavior of Πμ​ν\Pi^{\mu\nu} in several limits and materials.

Starting from the basis in Eq. 72, we include additional terms in the Lagrangian which account for the in-medium polarization tensor, here defined as Πμ​ν​(q)≡i​e2​⟨JEMμ​JEMν⟩\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q)\equiv ie^{2}\langle J^{\mu}_{\rm EM}J^{\nu}_{\rm EM}\rangle,

ℒ⊃\displaystyle{\cal L}\supset −14​F~μ​ν​F~μ​ν−14​Vμ​ν​Vμ​ν+12​mV2​Vμ​Vμ+e⁡(A~μ+κ​Vμ)​JEMμ+gχ​Vμ​JDμ\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4}\tilde{F}_{\mu\nu}\tilde{F}^{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{4}V_{\mu\nu}V^{\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{2}m_{V}^{2}V_{\mu}V^{\mu}+e(\tilde{A}_{\mu}+\kappa V_{\mu})J^{\mu}_{\rm EM}+g_{\chi}V_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{D}
−12​A~μ​Πμ​ν​A~ν−κ​A~μ​Πμ​ν​Vν.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\tilde{A}_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}\tilde{A}_{\nu}-\kappa\tilde{A}_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}V_{\nu}\,. (172)

In the limit that κ≪1\kappa\ll 1 and gχ≪1g_{\chi}\ll 1, we will drop terms in the Lagrangian of O⁡(κ2)O(\kappa^{2}) or O⁡(gχ2)O(g_{\chi}^{2}) and neglect the effect of any in-medium polarization tensor quadratic in VV. The polarization tensor Πμ​ν​(q)\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q) can be decomposed into longitudinal and transverse pieces:

Πμ​ν​(q)=ΠL​(q)​ηLμ​ηLν+ΠT​(q)​(η+μ)∗​η+ν+ΠT​(q)​(η−μ)∗​η−ν\displaystyle\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q)=\Pi_{L}(q)\eta_{L}^{\mu}\eta_{L}^{\nu}+\Pi_{T}(q)\,(\eta_{+}^{\mu})^{*}\,\eta_{+}^{\nu}+\Pi_{T}(q)\,(\eta_{-}^{\mu})^{*}\,\eta_{-}^{\nu} (173)

where q=(ω,𝐪)q=(\omega,{\bf q}). Taking 𝐪=|𝐪|​z^{\bf q}=|{\bf q}|\hat{z}, then the vectors above are defined as1010 10 Note that the ηL,T\eta_{L,T} here are a useful shorthand for decomposing the polarization tensor and satisfy qμ​Πμ​ν=0q_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}=0 as required for current conservation. They are not the same as the renormalized external photon polarization vectors.

ηLμ\displaystyle\eta_{L}^{\mu} =(1,0,0,ω|𝐪|)\displaystyle=\left(1,0,0,\frac{\omega}{|{\bf q}|}\right) (174)
η±μ\displaystyle\eta_{\pm}^{\mu} =12​(0,1,±i,0)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(0,1,\pm i,0) (175)

This general form of Πμ​ν​(q)\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q) thus satisfies the requirement of current conservation, and we have picked sign conventions for Πμ​ν\Pi^{\mu\nu} such that ΠT\Pi_{T} will correspond to a positive mass-squared contribution. Note that some references use a definition of ΠL\Pi_{L} which differs from this one by a factor of ΠL=q2/|𝐪|2​ΠLhere\Pi_{L}=q^{2}/|{\bf q}|^{2}\Pi_{L}^{\rm here} and Πμ​ν\Pi^{\mu\nu} is instead written in terms of a normalized longitudinal vector |𝐪|q2​(1,0,0,ω|𝐪|)\tfrac{|{\bf q}|}{\sqrt{q^{2}}}(1,0,0,\frac{\omega}{|{\bf q}|}). We follow here the convention of Ref. [227].

From Eq. 172, we can see that in-medium effects generate an effective mass for the photon, where the on-shell condition is defined by q2−ΠT​(q)=0q^{2}-\Pi_{T}(q)=0 for transverse modes and |𝐪|2−ΠL​(q)=0|{\bf q}|^{2}-\Pi_{L}(q)=0 for longitudinal modes. The solutions to these equations as well as the residues near the poles determine the in-medium dispersion relations ωL,T​(𝐪)\omega_{L,T}({\bf q}) as well as wavefunction renormalization for each polarization.
