However for |𝐪|≫ω|{\bf q}|\gg\omega, relevant for scattering processes, ΠL​(q)≈mD2​|𝐪|2/q2≈−mD2\Pi_{L}(q)\approx m_{D}^{2}|{\bf q}|^{2}/q^{2}\approx-m_{D}^{2} where mDm_{D} is the Debye mass. This is connected to the Debye screening of Coulomb scattering in a plasma; for an explicit expression of the Debye screening length λD=1/mD\lambda_{D}=1/m_{D}, see Eq. 190 below.

The in-medium mixing effects are important in determining constraints or searches for the dark photon portal. One set of important constraints on dark photons comes from stellar emission considerations. The dark photon can be emitted in the core of the star through the in-medium interactions above and escape due to the small couplings, leading to anomalous energy loss. This was studied recently in Refs. [119, 116, 118, 146, 117] for the Sun, red giants, horizontal branch stars, and SN1987a. Here the plasma mass in the core of the star ranges from ∼0.1−1\sim 0.1-1 keV (for the Sun or horizontal branch stars) up to ∼10\sim 10 MeV (for core collapse supernovae such as SN1987A).

We can use the in-medium couplings above to estimate the production of on-shell dark photons. As mentioned above, the real parts of the polarization tensors are Re​ΠT​(q)≈ωp2{\rm Re}\,\Pi_{T}(q)\approx\omega_{p}^{2} and Re​ΠL​(q)≈ωp2​|𝐪|2/ω2{\rm Re}\,\Pi_{L}(q)\approx\omega_{p}^{2}|{\bf q}|^{2}/\omega^{2} for the qq values relevant for this process. Meanwhile, the imaginary parts of the polarization tensors are proportional to the emission (and absorption) of photon modes in the medium, Im​ΠT​(q)≡−ω​ΓT{\rm Im}\,\Pi_{T}(q)\equiv-\omega\Gamma_{T} and Im​ΠL​(q)≡−(|𝐪|2/ω2)​ω​ΓL{\rm Im}\,\Pi_{L}(q)\equiv-(|{\bf q}|^{2}/\omega^{2})\omega\Gamma_{L}. Since Πμ​ν=i​e2​⟨JEMμ​JEMν⟩\Pi^{\mu\nu}=ie^{2}\langle J^{\mu}_{\rm EM}J^{\nu}_{\rm EM}\rangle, we can write the emission rate QQ of each dark photon polarization as

QT\displaystyle Q_{T} ∝−Im​ΠT​(q)​κ2​mV4(mV2−ωp2)2+(Im​ΠT​(q))2=κ2​mV4​ω​ΓT(mV2−ωp2)2+ω2​ΓT2\displaystyle\propto-{\rm Im}\,\Pi_{T}(q)\frac{\kappa^{2}m_{V}^{4}}{(m_{V}^{2}-\omega_{p}^{2})^{2}+({\rm Im}\,\Pi_{T}(q))^{2}}=\frac{\kappa^{2}m_{V}^{4}\,\omega\Gamma_{T}}{(m_{V}^{2}-\omega_{p}^{2})^{2}+\omega^{2}\Gamma_{T}^{2}} (184)
QL\displaystyle Q_{L} ∝−Im​ΠL​(q)​q2|𝐪|2​κ2​mV4(mV2−ωp2​q2/ω2)2+(Im​ΠL​(q)​q2/|𝐪|2)2=κ2​mV2​ω3​ΓL(ω2−ωp2)2+ω2​ΓL2\displaystyle\propto-{\rm Im}\,\Pi_{L}(q)\frac{q^{2}}{|{\bf q}|^{2}}\frac{\kappa^{2}m_{V}^{4}}{(m_{V}^{2}-\omega_{p}^{2}q^{2}/\omega^{2})^{2}+({\rm Im}\,\Pi_{L}(q)\,q^{2}/|{\bf q}|^{2})^{2}}=\frac{\kappa^{2}m_{V}^{2}\,\omega^{3}\Gamma_{L}}{(\omega^{2}-\omega_{p}^{2})^{2}+\omega^{2}\Gamma_{L}^{2}} (185)

where for the longitudinal polarization we used that q2=mV2q^{2}=m_{V}^{2} for on-shell production and the overall factor of q2/|𝐪|2q^{2}/|{\bf q}|^{2} comes from contracting Πμ​ν\Pi^{\mu\nu} with external polarization vectors ϵLμ=|𝐪|q2​(1,ω|𝐪|​𝐪^)\epsilon_{L}^{\mu}=\tfrac{|{\bf q}|}{\sqrt{q^{2}}}(1,\frac{\omega}{|{\bf q}|}\hat{\bf q}). While the detailed calculation of the production rate can be found in works such as Refs. [119, 118, 146], we highlight just a few things. First, there is resonant transverse polarization when mV=ωpm_{V}=\omega_{p}, but for mV≪ωpm_{V}\ll\omega_{p} the production rate scales as κ2​mV4\kappa^{2}m_{V}^{4}. For the longitudinal modes, there is resonant production for any mVm_{V} where ω=ωp\omega=\omega_{p} is kinematically possible. Furthermore, the process scales as κ2​mV2\kappa^{2}m_{V}^{2} and so this gives the dominant emission mechanism for mV≪ωpm_{V}\ll\omega_{p}. This explains why stellar emission constraints on κ\kappa scale as 1/mV1/m_{V} in the low mass limit. This mV2m_{V}^{2} suppression also means that ultralight vectors would not be efficiently produced in the early universe by interactions of SM charged particles, so there are no NeffN_{\rm eff} constraints on extra contributions to relativistic degrees of freedom.

B.1  Behavior of polarization tensor in various limits

The polarization tensor determines the in-medium dispersion relations as well as the optical properties of the medium. It is related to the dielectric function ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)\epsilon({\bf q},\omega) and conductivity σ⁡(𝐪,ω)\sigma({\bf q},\omega) by:

ϵT​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle\epsilon_{T}({\bf q},\omega) =1−ΠT​(q)ω2=1+i​σT​(𝐪,ω)ω\displaystyle=1-\frac{\Pi_{T}(q)}{\omega^{2}}=1+i\frac{\sigma_{T}({\bf q},\omega)}{\omega} (186)
ϵL​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle\epsilon_{L}({\bf q},\omega) =1−ΠL​(q)|𝐪|2=1+i​σL​(𝐪,ω)ω\displaystyle=1-\frac{\Pi_{L}(q)}{|{\bf q}|^{2}}=1+i\frac{\sigma_{L}({\bf q},\omega)}{\omega} (187)

Below we summarize the behavior of the real part of the polarization tensor. Meanwhile, the imaginary part determines absorption and emission rates via the optical theorem, Im​Π=−ω​Γ​(ω){\rm Im}\,\Pi=-\omega\Gamma(\omega) [229]. Ref. [228] provides more in-depth discussion, especially in the context of stellar environments.

For accurate in-medium dispersion relations, see Ref. [227], which explicitly gives Πμ​ν\Pi^{\mu\nu} in the regime where |𝐪|≃ω|{\bf q}|\simeq\omega. For a non-degenerate medium, a rough approximation when |𝐪|≃ω|{\bf q}|\simeq\omega is to take

ΠL​(q)\displaystyle\Pi_{L}(q) ≃ωp2−𝐪2\displaystyle\simeq\omega_{p}^{2}-{\bf q}^{2} (188)
ΠT​(q)\displaystyle\Pi_{T}(q) ≃ωp2\displaystyle\simeq\omega_{p}^{2} (189)

where ωp\omega_{p} is the plasma frequency. For a nonrelativistic electron gas, ωp2=ne​e2/me\omega_{p}^{2}=n_{e}e^{2}/m_{e}. For a relativistic and non-degenerate electron gas at temperature TT, ωp2=(e​T/3)2\omega_{p}^{2}=(eT/3)^{2}. (A simple model for the real and imaginary parts of ΠT,L\Pi_{T,L} in a metal is also discussed in Ref. [211].)

The limit of |𝐪|≫ω|{\bf q}|\gg\omega is relevant for nonrelativistic scattering processes. In this limit, Coulomb scattering via the longitudinal polarization dominates. In the classical limit (non-degenerate, non-relativistic gas),

ΠL​(q)≃−λD2=−ne​e2T≃−meT​ωp2\displaystyle\Pi_{L}(q)\simeq-\lambda_{D}^{2}=-\frac{n_{e}e^{2}}{T}\simeq-\frac{m_{e}}{T}\omega_{p}^{2} (190)

where λD\lambda_{D} is the Debye length and we have assumed an electron gas. In the degenerate limit,

ΠL​(q)≃−λTF2≃−4​α​EF​pFπ\displaystyle\Pi_{L}(q)\simeq-\lambda_{\rm TF}^{2}\simeq-\frac{4\alpha E_{F}p_{F}}{\pi} (191)

where λTF\lambda_{\rm TF} is the Thomas-Fermi screening length and EFE_{F} (pFp_{F}) is the energy (momentum) at the Fermi surface. For the complete dielectric function in the degenerate case, see Ref. [210] which reproduces the result from Ref. [230]. Ref. [230] provides useful derivations of ΠL,T\Pi_{L,T} from a materials point of view.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.
